The Woolly Mammoth’s Comeback Is Taking Longer Than Expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:28:55 UTC
04:28:55 KST

If you’ve been excitedly awaiting the return of the woolly mammoth, you’ll have to be patient a little longer. It was in 2021 that the newly established, Dallas-based company Colossal Biosciences announced plans to use modern gene-editing technology and DNA harvested from mammoth remains to manufacture a mammoth embryo, implant it in the womb of an elephant surrogate, and bring the great, gentle, six-ton beast—which vanished from the planet more than 4,000 years ago—back into the modern world. The target date for a pregnancy was 2027; the target date for the birth was 2028.
No more. In a recent conversation with TIME, Colossal CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm concedes that those goal posts have moved more than a little. “We are thinking it will be in the early 2030s,” he says. “We don’t have a hard date. Not 2036, but not 2030 either.”
In just the past year, Colossal has learned vastly more about both the mammoth and the elephant genomes than has ever been known before, not only improving the odds that the mammoth can be brought back to life, or de-extincted, but also unpacking basic genetic science that could one day have knock-on effects for humans—including potentially increasing resistance to cancer.
Bringing back the dire wolf
Colossal proved its de-extinction chops in the spring of 2025, when it announced that it had brought the extinct dire wolf back to life, editing the genome of the closely related gray wolf to replicate the features of its vanished cousin—including a white coat, larger size, more powerful shoulders, wider head, larger teeth and jaws, more-muscular legs, and characteristic vocalizations, especially howling and whining.
To work that genetic magic, Colossal scientists collected dire wolf DNA from an ear bone and a tooth unearthed in two ancient samples, sequenced the genome, and compared it to that of the gray wolf. They then harvested cells from a living gray wolf and made 20 edits on 14 genes using the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool, which produced the critical dire wolf characteristics. Finally, they extracted the nucleus of the edited cell, inserted it into a domestic dog ovum whose own nucleus had been removed, and implanted the resulting embryo into the womb of a domestic hound. Nine weeks later, the dire wolves were born.
Why woolly mammoths are so hard to de-extinct
To do something similar with the woolly mammoth, Colossal discovered that the work would be a heavier genetic lift than their research teams had originally expected. The initial estimate was that it would take edits to about 60 genes to turn an elephant nucleus into a mammoth nucleus that could then be used to create a mammoth embryo. Now that number is about 150—and rising.
Among the genes and regulatory switches that have been discovered are ones that shrink the mammoth ear to about one-tenth the size of an elephant’s ear. In the hot climates in which Asian and African elephants live, large, heavily vascularized ears serve as heat dumps, cooling the blood and the body as a whole. That would not do for the mammoth, which made its home during the Ice Age and needed to husband all the heat it could. Mammoth tails are shorter than those of elephants too— for the same heat-retention reason—and Colossal scientists have found the gene that expresses that as well.
The genetics of the mammoth’s characteristic heavy coat have also been unpacked. Nearly all hairy mammals—humans included—have oil-secreting glands known as sebaceous glands in the skin. The oil keeps individual hairs supple and prevents them from drying and breaking. Elephants, which have a very sparse covering of bristly hair across their bodies, were thought to be an exception to this rule. That made the job of engineering a mammoth from an elephant more difficult, since mammoths surely had sebaceous glands to sustain their extravagant coat. But Colossal researchers conducted dissection and close examination of samples of elephant skin and found that that earlier received wisdom was wrong—the skin does contain small, rudimentary sebaceous-like structures. The trick now is to isolate the genes that code for the glands and edit them to create the fully developed version the mammoth will need.
The researchers also analyzed the makeup of elephant hair and determined that 90% of every strand is composed of nine different proteins. They then tracked down which genes code for that protein production and govern hair developmental patterns, which typically include periods of growth, rest, and regrowth. Tests of these genes are underway, sometimes with the assistance of other animals.
In March 2025, Colossal revealed that it had created a small brood of 38 woolly mice, engineered with mammoth coding for shaggy hair written into their genome. The mice have thrived and bred, passing on their long, coarse hair to their pups. That was a good start, but mice aren’t mammoths, and to study how effective the genetic editing is, researchers will need to work with a larger mammal. Colossal promises that a woolly pig is coming, though the company does not say when it will be revealed.
Digging deeper into the genome of the mammoth, Colossal scientists have extracted bits of its regulatory DNA and inserted them into living elephant skin cells and watched as regulators turned the behavior of the genes up or down—critical work if you want to design other genes to order.
“It’s a little weird and Frankensteiny,” says Lamm, “but we’ve done that.”
Potential implications for humans
Colossal researchers are also exploring one of the elephant’s more remarkable features: its resistance to cancer. As a large-bodied mammal, elephants ought to be highly susceptible to the disease, especially considering that an elephant's body contains 100 times more cells than a human’s, creating more opportunities for cancer to occur. But cancer accounts for less than 5% of elephant deaths, compared to 16% for humans.
That was a longstanding mystery until recently. Both human and elephant cells are now known to carry a tumor-suppressor gene labeled TP53. When DNA in a cell is damaged—by cancer or other means—the gene codes for the release of the p53 protein, which either halts the damaged cell’s growth cycle to allow for repair, or, if the DNA is too corrupted, kills the cell. Humans carry two copies of the TP53 gene, while elephants carry 20—making for much greater cancer resistance. Additionally, elephants but not humans carry what is known as an LIF6 gene, which also produces a p53 protein, one that specifically targets the mitochondria—an energy-producing organelle located in the cellular cytoplasm—of damaged calls, killing them before they can divide and spread.
Other researchers are already exploring if p53 proteins can be manipulated in humans to increase cancer resistance. Colossal is casting a wider net. On August 20, it announced the launch of a new company, Astromech, which uses AI and deep learning to analyze the genomic data of any species, trace its evolutionary history, and forecast its future, anticipating its adaptation to changing environment, its disease susceptibility, and the possibility of so-called genetic bottlenecks—or lack of genetic diversity—that occur when an endangered population of animals grows too small. Colossal scientists are using Astromech to study elephants’ cancer resistance in depth—which could have broader uses and implications.
“Colossal is not conducting research on humans, but its work with mammoth, elephant, and other genomic datasets could yield insights relevant to human cancer research,” says a company spokesperson. “Understanding mechanisms such as elephants’ TP53-related cancer resistance is exactly the kind of problems Astromech is trying to understand, leveraging the mammoth, elephants and other datasets.”
For now, the goal of turning all of this scientific benchwork into a walking, breathing, breeding mammoth goes on—even if at a slower pace than originally predicted. “I hate to say this, because I don’t want to call the mammoth a product,” says Lamm, “but it will be a better product because of our deeper analysis of what truly made a mammoth a mammoth.”

US removes Syria from terrorism sponsor list, lifting major investment obstacle

US removes Syria from terrorism sponsor list, lifting major investment obstacle
DAMASCUS, Aug 24 - The United States removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism on Monday, lifting what Damascus says was the last major impediment to investing in the country as Washington deepens ties to the new Syrian government.
The removal, posted on the U.S. Treasury's website, took effect after a 45-day congressional review period triggered when Trump formally notified Congress on July 8 of his intention to rescind the designation.
“These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani told Reuters on Saturday that the government hoped removing what he called the "last obstacle" would help reconnect Syria to the global financial and economic system and boost investment. "There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.
Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups. The designation remained throughout the rule of his son Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by current President Ahmed al-Sharaa in December 2024.
CUBA, IRAN, NORTH KOREA REMAIN
Monday's announcement also removed the designation of the Nusrah Front as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization, leaving Cuba, Iran and North Korea as the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism.
The designation carries restrictions on U.S. foreign assistance, defense exports and sales, certain dual-use items and financial transactions, and had remained a major deterrent for banks and investors even after Washington dismantled its broader sanctions program on Syria.
Trump's administration terminated comprehensive U.S. sanctions on Syria in July 2025, while maintaining targeted sanctions against Assad and his associates, rights abusers, drug traffickers, Islamic State and al Qaeda affiliates and Iranian proxies.
The U.S. Treasury has since said American financial institutions can provide services to Syria, process payments involving Syrian banks and establish correspondent banking relationships with them, provided sanctioned parties are not involved.
But the terrorism designation remained a source of legal and compliance risk for firms considering entering Syria, whose government is seeking billions of dollars in investment to rebuild after nearly 14 years of war.
Signs of interest had grown ahead of the removal. Syria's finance ministry said this month that Finance Minister Mohammad Yisr Barnieh held talks with Bank of America executives over potential cooperation and Syria's reintegration into the international financial system. Bank officials expressed willingness to visit Syria and continue discussions, according to the ministry.
Mastercard has gone further, announcing in May that it was working with QNB Group and Syria's central bank to prepare infrastructure for international card payments in the country. The company has described itself as an early investor in Syria and said it wants to help connect Syrian consumers and businesses to global payment networks.
CONTINUED COOPERATION
Trump notified Congress of his decision after meeting Sharaa in Ankara in July, telling the Syrian president in a letter seen by Reuters that he had promised to "remove all barriers" preventing Syria from rebuilding.
The delisting also followed months of negotiations between Damascus and Washington over Syria's economic and foreign policy.
Reuters reported this month that Damascus agreed to drastically reduce imports of Russian oil during discussions with Washington over lifting the terrorism designation, according to three sources familiar with the talks.
Trump has increasingly embraced Sharaa, the former commander of al Qaeda's Nusra Front who broke ties with the global jihadist network in 2016 and led the rebel coalition that overthrew Assad.
Washington has praised cooperation by Sharaa's government against Islamic State and said easing restrictions is intended to give Syria an opportunity to stabilise, attract investment and rebuild. REUTERS

Reuters: Ukrainian drones knocked out a major Russian oil refinery in Perm for the second time this year
The oil refinery in Perm has halted operations following a Ukrainian drone attack, two industry sources told Reuters. The sources said repairs could take up to two weeks.
Ukrainian forces struck Perm with drones on the morning of August 21. Journalists later reported smoke rising over the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez plant. The sources confirmed to Reuters that the attack caused a fire at the refinery.
One of the plant’s primary crude distillation units, which accounts for about 40% of the refinery’s capacity, has been shut down, according to Reuters. A second primary unit, which accounts for 34% of capacity, has been idle since July 29, the sources said.
Ukrainian drones have struck the Perm refinery several times since the spring of 2026. In early May, the plant had already halted operations indefinitely.
Permnefteorgsintez is one of Russia’s largest oil refineries. It ranks seventh in the country by refining volume, according to Reuters.
Repeated Ukrainian strikes on oil industry facilities have kept Russia in a fuel crisis all summer. A new wave of the crisis began in mid-August: gasoline prices are rising, and regions across the country are imposing limits on sales.

No Tanks, No Troops—Ukraine Sends Its Robot Army Through Kyiv in World-First Drone Parade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:28:06 UTC
04:28:06 KST

- Category

No Tanks, No Troops—Ukraine Sends Its Robot Army Through Kyiv in World-First Drone Parade
Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day with a radically different kind of military display, sending combat robots down Kyiv’s main street, naval drones across the Dnipro River and UAVs into the skies in what Defence Blog described as the world’s first military parade centered entirely on unmanned systems.
The August 24 demonstration replaced the traditional columns of tanks, armored vehicles and marching troops with some of the technologies that have come to define Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s full-scale invasion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Dozens of unmanned ground vehicles rolled along Khreshchatyk in central Kyiv, showcasing robotic platforms designed for combat, reconnaissance, logistics and other frontline missions.
On the Dnipro River, Ukrainian naval drones including the Magura and Sea Baby were displayed. Both families of unmanned vessels have become closely associated with Ukraine’s campaign against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet.
The maritime display included reconnaissance platforms, strike drones and versions equipped with air defense missiles, demonstrating how Ukraine has expanded the role of unmanned vessels far beyond their original use as explosive attack craft.
Ukrainian drones also appeared above the capital, including reconnaissance systems, strike UAVs and interceptor drones developed to destroy incoming Russian aerial threats.
The display offered a snapshot of how deeply Ukraine’s military has changed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Drones that initially played mostly supporting roles have evolved into central elements of Ukrainian operations on land, at sea and in the air. Kyiv has since institutionalized that transformation by creating the Unmanned Systems Forces as a dedicated branch of its military.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed legislation establishing the branch in 2024, making Ukraine the first country to build a separate military service specifically around unmanned warfare. June 11 has since been designated as the annual Day of the Unmanned Systems Forces.
The Independence Day demonstration brought many of those technologies together in the center of the Ukrainian capital.
Ukraine had not staged a conventional military parade during the full-scale war. In previous years, Khreshchatyk instead became known for displays of destroyed Russian tanks, armored vehicles and other equipment captured or knocked out during fighting.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukraine is expanding its fleet of unmanned ground vehicles, aiming to produce at least 50,000 combat and logistics robots this year to reinforce infantry units and bridge manpower shortages along the frontline.

“We now have to operate under funding constraints,” Zelensky said, adding that “one of the main options is to provide funds from the European loan ahead of schedule, already this year.”

Patriot interceptors remain a priority as Ukraine continues to prepare for the upcoming autumn and winter.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir delivered separate statements on Monday evening after the discovery of the Altalena, the ship sunk off Israel’s coast during the War of Independence, with the event overshadowed by a dispute between the two coalition partners over credit for the discovery.

According to Maariv, the two had been expected to make a joint statement, and decided at the last minute to separate.
Associates of Ben-Gvir said that “the prime minister’s conduct shows his intention to go with [Gadi] Eisenkot. Ben-Gvir was good for him for four years, and now, of all times, to return to boycotts and avoid even taking a picture with him?! This is exactly what they did to Menachem Begin, and it is regrettable that the prime minister is behaving this way toward a coalition partner.”
Netanyahu's press conference was held at the Etzel Museum following the discovery of the shipwreck. The prime minister said he intends to raise the Altalena from the depths of the sea and turn it into “a tangible symbol” for current and future generations, centered on the message: “Civil war, never again!”
“Civil war, never! That was the heartfelt call of Etzel commander Menachem Begin," Netanyahu continued. "He stood here on the shore, not far from here, and he said these words following David Ben-Gurion’s tragic decision to open fire on the rescue ship ‘Altalena.’”
The prime minister said that “the ship brought significant weapons for our soldiers during the War of Independence. But instead of unloading these vital weapons, the ‘Haganah’ members on the shore opened a barrage of fire on the ‘Altalena’ that claimed the lives of 16 Etzel fighters and three IDF soldiers.”
Netanyahu said that every year since then, Altalena supporters have gathered for a memorial ceremony honoring those who fell and their comrades who later died in the War of Independence.
“They were not bitter; they did not say, ‘They opened fire on us, we will not fight.’ They went and fought together with their comrades in the ‘Haganah’ in the ranks of the IDF during the War of Independence.”
He added: “From the ranks of the IDF during the War of Independence, I come to this ceremony and salute them,” saying that “in recent years, something absurd has happened. During the ceremony, I hear calls of incitement against us by political rivals standing outside the ceremony and simply desecrating it. Have they not learned the lesson? We are brothers, political rivals, but we are brothers, sons of one nation with one future and one destiny.”
The prime minister also said that in recent years he had asked education ministers to include the Altalena story in the curriculum.
'Today, finally, after 78 years, we have located the ship'
Netanyahu added that he had also worked to preserve Israel’s historical heritage, saying he established the Heritage Directorate in the Prime Minister’s Office in 2009 and later set as a goal the search for the Altalena. He said an initial search effort was carried out in 2011 together with the Begin Center, but failed to locate the ship, before the search was renewed in 2019 with a dedicated budget and based on the diary of the ship’s captain, Emanuel Fein.
“Today, finally, after 78 years, we have located the ship after it sank into the depths,” Netanyahu said.
“I congratulate Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu and all the people who took part in this operation. This is a moving moment, a warming moment. Off the coast of Tel Aviv, the Altalena went up in flames. This is the great lesson of the Altalena: division is weakness and unity is strength. The unity among us is broader than it appears. Therefore, we must establish a broad national government.”
Netanyahu described the discovery as a historic moment, saying: “Off the coast of Tel Aviv, the Altalena went up in flames; off the coast of Tel Aviv, brothers fell by the hands of brothers. But precisely out of the infernal fire, burst forth the immortal cry of the commander of the Etzel, Menachem Begin of blessed memory, to stop the firing that was taking place, to stop the entire course of the battle, because we will not go to a civil war.”
'Against our enemies, we do not hesitate'
Ben-Gvir later gave his own statement to the media.
“The Altalena is not just a ship. It is a symbol of the national camp that for years they tried to boycott, silence, and remove from legitimacy. Menachem Begin knew what persecution by brothers meant, what a boycott meant, and what it feels like when they try to disqualify you and the camp you represent. And yet, precisely at the most difficult moment, he established one principle above all: We are brothers. There will be no civil war,” he said.
Ben-Gvir further said that for decades, “they tried to bury the story of the Altalena, remove it from the pages of history, and erase the legacy of the heroes who fought and fell. The search for the ship’s remains is not only an operation to locate remains in the depths of the sea. For us, this is a moral and values-based obligation. Sixteen heroic Etzel fighters fell aboard it, and the remains that were discovered are part of their memorial and their legacy.”
The minister added that the discovery also represented a personal closing of a circle for him.
“My mother, Shoshana, may she rest in peace, was a proud Etzel fighter. In the home where I grew up, I absorbed stories of heroism, but also stories of persecution and discrimination,” he said.
“The lesson of the Altalena is true today as well: Against our enemies, we do not hesitate, we do not show mercy, and we are not confused, but strike them with all our might. But within our own people, even when there are deep disagreements, the testament of Begin is clear: Jews, in all their forms, are brothers. There will be no civil war.”

2 children among 4 killed in Gaza a week after US asked Israel to curb attacks

2 children among 4 killed in Gaza a week after US asked Israel to curb attacks
DEIR AL-BALAH, Gaza Strip (AP) — Palestinian residents of war-battered Gaza fled homes and businesses as Israeli strikes and tank fire killed at least four people Monday, including two children, hospital officials said, a week after a U.S. delegation asked Israel to draw down attacks.
After evacuation warnings by Israel’s military, a strike hit a building in the Bureij refugee camp in central Gaza. One family was unable to flee and a 4-year-old child was killed, according to Awda Hospital, where he was taken. His mother and sister were wounded. There was no Israeli military comment.
Israeli strikes hit three other buildings across the territory after residents said they received evacuation warnings. Some people sprinted away, with mothers carrying children, while others moved amid the rubble in wheelchairs or with canes.
Smoke rose over the already devastated landscape.
Israel’s military said it carried out strikes in the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City and in Deir al-Balah after issuing warnings, targeting what it described as two Hamas weapons storage facilities inside mosques. The military did not provide evidence but said the facilities contained dozens of “Kalashnikov rifles, magazines and additional military equipment.”
An earlier Israeli strike on a tent in Deir al-Balah killed a man, according to Al-Aqsa Hospital, where his body was taken. Israel’s military said it killed a militant affiliated with Hamas’ special forces unit.
Others were killed or hurt in Khan Younis in the south
A man was killed and five others were wounded in an Israeli strike in Khan Younis in southern Gaza, according to Nasser Hospital, which received the casualties.
And Israeli tank fire hit an area east of Khan Younis, killing a 10-year-old girl, according to the hospital, where her body was taken.
Israel’s military did not immediately comment on the strike in Khan Younis and said it was not aware of the incident with the child.
Israel has continued to carry out targeted killings in the week since a U.S. delegation met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in an effort to push last year’s ceasefire deal forward.
U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner asked Netanyahu to draw down Israel’s attacks in Gaza, a person familiar with the meeting said last week, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief journalists.
Israel has announced strikes on six of the seven days since that meeting.
Israel says it is targeting militants and related sites
While the heaviest fighting in Gaza has subsided since the ceasefire took hold in October, Israeli airstrikes have killed at least 1,288 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s health ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-led government, maintains detailed casualty records that are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not give a breakdown of civilians and militants.
Militants have carried out shooting attacks on Israeli troops, and Israel says its strikes are in response to that and other ceasefire violations. Five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire.
Palestinian officials have reported strikes on homes and police stations, and Hamas has claimed that attacks are designed to destabilize Gaza and prevent progress on the ceasefire’s next steps, which include demilitarizing and reconstructing the territory and the deployment of an international stabilization force.
Israel warns against kites sent from Gaza
In the period before the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel that sparked the war, burning kites and balloons were sent from Gaza into Israel, causing fires and other damage.
Now Israeli officials are expressing concern after several kites were found in a kibbutz near Gaza. No weapons or dangerous materials were attached. Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz in a statement Sunday threatened to ramp up strikes on Gaza unless Hamas ensures the kites stop flying toward Israel.
Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem has called the kites “essentially children’s toys” and accused Israel of using them as “an attempt to justify the continuation of aggression and violations against our people.”
The Oct. 7 attack killed some 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. All hostages or their remains were later released. Israel’s retaliatory offensive in Gaza has killed more than 73,422 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
___
AlJoud reported from Beirut. AP writer Sam Metz in Jerusalem contributed to this report.

Earth is simmering in its hottest water temps on record, and that’s bad for fish and us
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:23:02 UTC
04:23:02 KST

Earth is simmering in its hottest water temps on record, and that’s bad for fish and us
The European climate service Copernicus says the world’s oceans have reached their hottest temperature on record. This increase is driven by a strong El Nino and human-caused climate change. (AP Video by Teresa de Miguel)
The world’s oceans simmered to their hottest temperatures on record over the weekend and are likely to warm even further in the next few months, putting stress on life in the water and on land too, the European climate service Copernicus announced Monday.
Spurred by a still growing but already supersized natural El Nino and human-caused climate change, the world’s ocean temperatures hit 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit) on Friday and Saturday, narrowly edging out the average daily record set in March 2024, said Samantha Burgess, strategic climate lead for Copernicus.
“This is yet another sign of our climate system under strain and the ocean under immense pressure,” Burgess said.
Jane Lubchenco, an oceanographer and former chief of the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration called the record “very troubling.”
“An ocean this warm destabilizes weather patterns and threatens food security, economic prosperity and marine life,” Lubchenco said in an email. “A warmer ocean is not our friend.”
Warmer water means worse storms, hotter nights
When the ocean warms it becomes more acidic and carries less oxygen which hurts food industries that rely on the seas, Burgess said. It also changes ocean currents and weather patterns, giving more juice to storms to make them rainier and make storm surge bigger, Burgess said.
“When we have a warmer ocean such as we’ve had in Europe this summer, it amplifies the impact of heat waves because you don’t get the cooler nighttime temperatures with the sea breeze coming off the ocean when the ocean is very warm,” Burgess said.
Normally, because most of the Southern Hemisphere is ocean, the world’s sea surface temperature peaks in March and April, as the southern summer draws to a close. But this year, the record was set in August, Burgess said. So the oceans will keep getting hotter until the current El Nino — a natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that then warps weather and raises temperatures globally — reaches its peak, which is expected sometime between November and January, she said.
El Nino is already as big as recent ones and is still growing with it expected to reach unprecedented levels at its peak. It’s responsible for a good chunk of the heat in the oceans, and long-term warming from the burning of coal, oil and gas has warmed the waters by 0.8 degrees Celsius (1.4 degrees Fahrenheit), Burgess said.
“The thing that makes my heart sink is that this starts so early and it’s so out-of-normal that you know when it hits its peak, it’s going to be unprecedented,” said Boris Worm, a biology professor at Canada’s Dalhousie University. “The ocean is not supposed to do this.”
“It’s just that there is no normal anymore,” Worm said.
Hot water kills coral, anchovies
“It’s frightening,” said University of North Carolina marine ecologist John Bruno. “We’re not even in October yet. You know, usually the Caribbean peaks at like late September, early October. And I think next year in the Southern Ocean, the Great Barrier Reef, yeah I’m really worried about what’s going to happen in the southern hemisphere in February, March.”
The amount of heat sensitive coral alive today is about one-fifth of 1990s levels, Bruno said. But lately scientists have found that some species of coral — more the “weedy” kinds not the long-lived iconic kind like staghorn — are adapting to the hotter water and it’s not quite the wipe-out event once feared, he said.
Bruno and Worm warned of fisheries collapse and food shortages.
They both mentioned the largest fishery in the world, the Peruvian anchovy fishery. That usually collapses during El Nino and is especially likely with this heat, Worm said. And that alters the food web because larger fish, marine mammals and seabirds feed on them.
When the water gets hot, larger creatures can swim to cooler water, going halfway across an ocean, but “anchovies can’t leave so they just don’t reproduce or starve,” Worm said. And the seabirds and even humans who depend on them are affected.
With hotter water, “not everybody is hit equally, obviously, but the whole system collapses,” Worm said. “It’s like when you pull out the rug from underneath an economy. It’s, like, the whole thing collapses. Some sectors may do a little bit better, but overall, everybody suffers.”
Burgess said as the waters warm off Europe, people are seeing more jellyfish and, Bruno said, the same thing could be happening on the U.S. East Coast.
“Jellyfish are often opportunistic and they like warm waters,” Worm said. “So yes, I would expect them to do a little bit better.”
Another former NOAA chief, Rick Spinrad, said the ocean is the planet’s thermostat, so “as long as we depend on a healthy ocean for our safety, prosperity and wellbeing, these record-breaking sea surface temperatures portend even greater challenges for us all.”

Russian chess teams barred from 2026 Olympiad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

04:22:02 KST

Russian chess teams barred from 2026 Olympiad
The International Chess Federation (FIDE) has barred Russian teams from returning to the Chess Olympiad next month, prompting prominent names in Russian chess to accuse its leadership of politicizing the sport and making “Russophobic” decisions.
FIDE suspended the Russian and Belarusian national teams from its competitions in 2022, although players from both countries were allowed to compete individually under neutral status. The federation lifted all restrictions on Belarusian athletes last month.
On Sunday, the FIDE Council ruled that Russian teams would remain excluded from the 46th Chess Olympiad, which is scheduled to take place in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, from September 16 to 27.
Russian Chess Federation chief Aleksandr Tkachev said the decision had undermined FIDE’s own motto, “We are one family,” and accused members of the Council of putting their personal interests ahead of chess.
“There are people who prioritize the game over politics and don’t worry about their own careers. But there are also people who prioritize personal interests, and they currently predominate on the Council. This time, they prevailed,” Tkachev told TASS on Monday.
He claimed the decision had been initiated by acting FIDE President Viswanathan Anand, who took over last month after his Russian predecessor, Arkady Dvorkovich, was forced to step aside after he was placed under EU sanctions.
Russian chess legend Anatoly Karpov, the 12th world champion, went further, accusing the federation’s leadership of Russophobia.
“There is only one explanation for this decision – the FIDE leadership has gotten out of control. The decisions being made are Russophobic,” Karpov told TASS. “Let’s hope the situation changes after the elections in September.”
FIDE is due to hold its presidential election in Uzbekistan on September 26-27, alongside the closing stages of the Olympiad.
The ruling means Russia will miss its third consecutive over-the-board Olympiad after being absent from Chennai in 2022 and Budapest in 2024.
Former FIDE president Kirsan Ilyumzhinov said he was “ashamed” of the decision, arguing that sport should remain above politics.
Russian players nevertheless remain prominent internationally under the FIDE flag. They won four medals – one gold, two silvers and one bronze – at the Asian rapid and blitz championships in Hong Kong last month.
Moscow has repeatedly condemned restrictions imposed on Russian athletes by international sporting bodies as politically motivated. President Vladimir Putin has argued that comparable measures have not been applied to athletes from other countries involved in armed conflicts.

Ukraine, UK sign landmark AI deal

Ukraine, UK sign landmark AI deal
Ukrinform reports this with reference to the UK government.
The AI partnership agreement, signed in Kyiv by President Volodymyr Zelensky and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, will give Ukraine access to support from world-leading universities, researchers and technology companies, as well as the world's third-largest AI ecosystem.
The UK is set to become the first international partner to gain access to Ukraine's Avengers AI Labs, enabling the two countries to accelerate the development of AI tools designed to shape the battlefield.
“By combining Ukrainian battlefield data with British expertise, we will accelerate the development of capabilities that not only strengthen our national security but better protect our critical infrastructure and growth in every postcode here at home,” the UK government said.
The platform provides real world data and insights to train AI models, collected by thousands of daylight cameras and infrared sensors across the battlefield in Ukraine.
These sensors and cameras capture millions of objects, including tanks, artillery, air defense systems, infantry and aerial targets such as Shahed drones and reconnaissance UAVs, feeding the data into Avengers AI Labs to train new AI models.
Under the partnership, the UK and Ukraine will also explore other platforms for cooperation.
The UK government described Avengers AI Labs as “a goldmine of battlefield data” that will give British innovators and researchers unprecedented access to real operational data and the ability to rapidly develop and test new technologies.
In turn, the UK will provide Ukraine with access to world-leading universities, researchers, technology companies and its extensive AI ecosystem, enabling Ukraine to draw on British expertise to accelerate the development of solutions to urgent challenges and turn hard-won battlefield experience and unique datasets into technologies that will benefit both countries.
“This groundbreaking partnership will bring together Ukraine’s unrivalled operational experience with Britain’s world-class AI ecosystem, giving us the opportunity to develop the technologies of the future, changing lives here in Britain and saving lives on the battlefield in Ukraine,” Prime Minister Burnham said.
“Ukraine has become one of the world’s leading innovators in defence technology, forged through courage, ingenuity and the hard lessons of war,” he added.
As reported, during his first foreign trip as Prime Minister, Burnham assured Ukraine that he would work to strengthen assistance to the country, particularly in air defense and countering Russian missile strikes.
Earlier, the UK government announced that it would allow European defense company MBDA to declassify information on British components used in Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles for Ukraine.

Ben Gurion Airport chaos foreseen: Officials warned of manpower shortages and safety risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:18:17 UTC
04:18:17 KST

Minutes from a meeting of senior managers in the operations division of the Israel Airports Authority, held four days before operations at Ben Gurion Airport were halted, show that senior authority officials were aware of a severe manpower shortage affecting the airport’s operation during the summer season.
The meeting addressed a gap in the desired number of employees recruited, the burnout of the existing workforce and a resulting rise in safety incidents. The airport’s fire chief and the official responsible for first aid said they did not have the capacity to respond in emergency situations.
The workers’ committee, headed by Pinchas Idan, published two days ago a “Situation report on the manpower shortage at the Israel Airports Authority.” According to the report, the authority is short 400 to 500 workers across all divisions. The authority dismissed the document, responding: “The figures change from one publication to the next, all in an attempt to retroactively justify the serious and unnecessary harm caused to the traveling public.” However, the minutes indicate that various officials had raised the problems that peaked on Thursday.
One manager said at the meeting that “there has been an increase in safety incidents due to the manpower gap” and asked those present to do what was necessary to reduce them: “It is your responsibility to disseminate and discuss the incidents, including their implications, with every last employee.”
He also noted that the airport was at the height of the summer season: “In August there will be 2.6 million passengers, September will stand at around 2.5 million passengers, with the highest number of passengers ever at Ben Gurion Airport in this month. I am impressed by the work of the management team and the units, all of whom are mobilized for the summer.”
The Ben Gurion Airport fire chief warned at the meeting: “The administration’s conduct is problematic, which is why we have reached this situation. Aviation regulations will take effect in November and despite the fact that we have raised and highlighted the issue, I am warning that we are not prepared for an aviation emergency and do not meet operational readiness requirements, including understaffing on shifts. We are committed to providing a response and I feel that I do not have the ability to provide that response if several incidents occur simultaneously.”
The official responsible for first aid added: “This week there was a discussion regarding manpower, about the shortage of an additional ambulance driver, and this affects the department’s ability to respond during an emergency. We are short five paramedics and there is no possibility of staffing Terminal 1, including the issue of not sending people to paramedic training.”
A senior official in the ground services division said that “the recruitment system and the transfer of employees between divisions will eventually collapse.” According to him, “The status of managers in the organization is low. There are excellent people in the division and if a manager says, ‘It won’t happen,’ that needs to be respected. Otherwise, we have to deal with the consequences. As a manager, I take responsibility, including for professional recommendations — and we are not respected. We did not receive the Production Council’s minutes and this created a problem for us. In my opinion, this is where the gap in employee recruitment stems from.”
A senior official in the operations department warned: “The serious incident will come. I am raising a red flag about the safety incidents. The statement about performing miracles is problematic. The veteran workforce is exhausted and the new workforce is unskilled. Operational equipment is not being maintained and aircraft are being assigned to unsuitable positions under risk management. This has been going on for a long time. The flight schedule is essentially a ‘recommendation’ for ground service companies and airlines, and requests for changes place a burden on the division’s other units, including last-minute tail connections.”
One of the senior managers in the operations division responded: “I am aware, and I am asking that we stop situations in real time when it is impossible to proceed and the risk is unacceptable. Send the data and we will hold a discussion on the matter, including consideration of solutions. I disagree with the statement regarding the flight schedule. Each airline received a letter from the airport manager before disciplinary proceedings. Actions are being taken and I agree that we have not reached the place we want to be.
“Regarding the fire department staffing standard, 16 firefighters per shift have been set, including the recruitment of 15 additional firefighters. A discussion is scheduled with the deputy director of administration and the airport manager.”
Operations at Ben Gurion Airport came to a halt on Thursday. Dozens of flights were canceled and hundreds more were delayed. About 100,000 passengers were affected by the disruptions, while the Finance Ministry estimated the damage to the economy at about 30 million shekels (about $8.5 million). Israel Airports Authority management blamed the workers’ committee for “work disruptions,” while the committee rejected the claim that it was a planned strike.
The Israel Airports Authority had not responded as of publication.

Türkiye on Monday established four subcommissions to coordinate implementation of legislation aimed at strengthening national unity and social cohesion, according to a board overseeing the process.

It said the law was adopted by the Turkish Parliament with “a high level of social and political consensus” and reflected the will of the Turkish people.
“Türkiye will continue to implement these historic steps with determination, in full coordination among all its institutions, to strengthen social integration,” the board said.

General Atomics Aeronautical Systems predicts the new drone it plans to pitch for the military’s “Massed Modular Aircraft” program will exceed many of the military’s requirements for a successor to the MQ-9 Reaper.
Wildfire, as General Atomics has dubbed it, “meets every wish on the [MMA] list and exceeds most of them,” company spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a statement, though he declined to specify the drone’s expected capabilities or cost. Aviation Week first reported the company’s plans for Wildfire.

The Defense Innovation Unit released a solicitation July 7 asking companies to submit ideas for the new drone concept, which is meant “to execute missions that the MQ-9A performs today.”
The Air Force is partnering with DIU on the MMA effort, which it said “will directly inform the requirements for the MQ-9’s successor.”
DIU’s solicitation called for drones to be able to carry a payload of at least 2,800 pounds—roughly the weight of one Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile, or LRASM—and have an unrefueled combat radius of at least 2,300 nautical miles, while carrying a payload, as well as being able to fly a one-way ferrying flight of at least 8,000 nautical miles.
The Pentagon wants MMA drones to be able to launch weapons, collect intelligence, conduct electronic warfare, or relay communications while staying airborne for long periods. DIU said that is intended to exhaust an enemy and force them to burn through pricey anti-aircraft missiles and other resources.
While General Atomics did not detail what Wildfire—a medium-altitude long endurance drone—will be able to do, Brinkley’s statement hinted at some of the goals the company set out to achieve.
“How do we come out of the box, day one, with a 10,000 nautical mile ferry range?” Brinkley said. “Can we carry four LRASMs? Can we swarm 100 aircraft under semi-autonomous control? Can we fuse all of that data into a highly effective common operating picture? Can we do that at scalable, affordable mass?”
The Air Force has lost dozens of MQ-9 drones since operations against Iran launched in late February. The Washington Post reported earlier in August that about 45 Reapers have been lost, in some cases shot down, during Operation Epic Fury.
In its original solicitation, DIU said that with adversaries increasingly using low-cost antiaircraft capabilities to create layered defenses, the military won’t be able to rely on “exquisite” aircraft with price tags north of $30 million. For that reason, DIU and the Air Force said, the military needs drone capabilities that can weather some losses while still being able to accomplish their missions.
The Air Force and DIU want these new drones to be modular so they can be quickly updated with payloads like full-motion video sensors, so an MMA could carry out some of the MQ-9’s current missions. An Air Force official told reporters earlier in August that the service wants to start awarding contracts by the end of this year.
DIU also wants contractors to be able to flight test a full-scale prototype 21 months after receiving the award and to be able to deliver 20 mission-ready aircraft by fiscal 2031.
Brinkley said General Atomics “can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the current schedule.”
However, Brinkley said, the military has an “immediate, critical ISR gap” that Wildfire would not be able to fill in the short term. General Atomics has options that could serve as an interim bridge, he said, and the company is now discussing those with Pentagon decision-makers.
General Atomics did not reveal any imagery or concept art for Wildfire.

'We need more money' — Zelensky says Kyiv needs to produce hundreds more drones per day to pressure Russia into peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:14:15 UTC
04:14:15 KST

'We need more money' — Zelensky says Kyiv needs to produce hundreds more drones per day to pressure Russia into peace
Ukraine needs additional financing in order to dramatically increase its daily drone production and maintain a competitive edge with Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 24 during a press conference at the Coalition of the Willing summit Kyiv.
Thirty officials and leaders from the European Union and NATO countries gathered for a meeting in support of Ukraine on the country's 35th Independence Day — its fifth since the start of Russia's full-scale war.
When asked about Ukraine's capacity to continue launching deep strikes against Russia to pressure the Kremlin to the negotiating table, Zelensky said Kyiv's challenge is not capacity, but funding.
"We have enough capacity, of course, to increase the production, and if we will increase the production, we will be able to attack more. ... but we don't have enough financing for this," the president said.
Russia has increased the number of Shahed-type drones it launches at Ukraine, now attacking with up to 1,000 UAVs a day in mass strikes, Zelensky said. In order to "bring back this war to Russia and make it painful," Kyiv needs to scale up its daily production to match Moscow.
"We need the same competitive number," he said.
Ukraine is currently producing around 200-300 drones per day, according to Zelensky. Kyiv can triple that total with less money than Moscow uses for its drone industry — 140 million euros compared to Russia's 340 million — but that still requires a bigger budget than Ukraine has now.
"We need more money, much more," Zelensky said.
read also
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who participated in the Coalition of the Willing meeting, said he agreed that Ukraine needs more funding to increase deep strikes against Russia, and that continuing to launch deep strikes was "a sensible military strategy."
To end the war, Kyiv's allies will need "to give military and financial support to Ukraine to increase its capacity for deep strikes,whether with missiles or with drones," Stubb said.
"And the reason for this is very simple. It increases the cost and the price of the war for Russia. ... this is the only way we're going to get into the peace negotiations at the table."
Russia has intensified the scale and frequency of its mass missile and drone attacks against Ukraine in spring and summer 2026, making this period one of the deadliest for civilians since the first days of the full-scale invasion.
In late March 2026, Russia for the first time launched nearly 1,000 drones at Ukraine in one day, breaking its previous record.
Recent mass strikes against Ukrainian cities have seen 500 Shahed-type drones launched in a single attack.
Shahed-type drones — Iranian-designed, with a Russian-produced version known as Geran-2 — have become a central weapon in Moscow's strike arsenal, valued for their ability to carry large warheads.
Often painted black to make them less visible at night, Gerans can cover about 2,500 kilometers (1,554 miles) and reach speeds of up to 180 kilometers per hour (112 miles per hour), according to Ukraine's military intelligence.
Russia has continued modifying and modernizing the Shahed model throughout the full-scale war, now escalating its use of deadlier, more destructive jet-powered drones in aerial bombardments.

Joey Manu has revealed how a conversation with Papua New Guinea's prime minister helped convince him to return to the NRL and join the Chiefs in 2028.

ALBAWABA- Yemen’s Houthi group on Monday claimed responsibility for a ballistic-missile strike on the Saudi-flagged oil tanker Amzan in the Red Sea off Yanbu, escalating its campaign against Saudi-linked shipping and threatening a key route for the kingdom’s oil exports.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the tanker was hit directly, causing a fire and prompting nearby vessels to leave the area. The group said the attack was part of its declared blockade of Saudi-linked maritime traffic and its policy of “blockade for blockade.”
Saudi shipping company Bahri confirmed that the Amzan was involved in a security incident in the Red Sea but did not attribute responsibility for the attack. It said all crew members were safe and that no injuries had been reported. The Houthis also claimed two separate attacks against Saudi-backed forces inside Yemen. According to their statement, ballistic missiles and drones targeted a large military convoy in the Al-Abr and Al-Wadi'ah areas, allegedly destroying more than 10 trucks carrying weapons and military equipment.
A second operation targeted Saudi-aligned forces in Al-Kanais, with the Houthis claiming casualties among commanders and officers and the destruction of weapons depots. Local sources confirmed the strikes and reported that vehicles belonging to civilians were burned as a result of the Houthi attack on the Wadi’ah area.
The latest escalation comes amid a broader deterioration in Yemen’s fragile security environment. The conflict had remained largely frozen since the 2022 UN-brokered truce, but tensions have intensified in recent weeks amid renewed Saudi-Houthi confrontation and stalled Omani-mediated efforts to reach a political settlement.
The escalation also coincides with the wider US-Iran confrontation and disruptions to regional shipping. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on Red Sea routes such as Yanbu to move oil while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted.

US launches 'operation economic outcast' as Washington targets Iran's 'enablers'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:11:00 UTC
04:11:00 KST

"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday.
The United States is launching what it has branded "Operation Economic Outcast" against Iran as Washington seeks to sever Tehran's financial lifelines amid the ongoing war.
In a press conference on Monday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent outlined a new, "unprecedented campaign" against Iran and its "enablers," describing it as an "economic onslaught" aimed at isolating the Iranian regime.
"Treasury has mapped every node, every facilitator, and every network that Iran has used to smuggle oil and evade sanctions," he said. "Beginning today, the actions of Treasury and other agencies will tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue that funds the IRGC and the evil Iranian regime".
"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system," he continued, adding that US President Donald Trump was contacting unspecified world leaders requesting that they stop working with Iran.
As part of the campaign, the Treasury Department announced on Monday that it had also "issued determinations against five critical sectors - digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping - that the Iranian regime uses to try to prop up its failing economy."
Moving forward, Bessent said Iran was now left with "a very clear choice."
"Complete global isolation and a subsistence economy, or a path back to normalcy, with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy".
Bessent's warning comes around six months after US and Israeli strikes on Iran marked the beginning of the war in the region, which the Trump administration says aims to ensure Iran can never obtain a nuclear weapon.
The conflict has largely ground to a stalemate in recent months, with negotiations faltering and a growing dispute over the Strait of Hormuz.
The strategic waterway, a crucial oil and gas transit chokepoint that connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, has been a sticking point in talks between Washington and Tehran, with both sides claiming control over the passage.

European gas prices hit highest level since January 2023 amid Iran sanctions concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:09:24 UTC
04:09:24 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
European natural gas prices climbed nearly 4% on Monday to their highest level since January 2023 after the US launched a sweeping campaign to isolate Iran from the global financial system, heightening concerns over further disruptions to Middle Eastern energy supplies.
The September futures contract at Dutch-based TTF, Europe’s benchmark gas trading hub, rose around 4% to €68.45 ($79.85) per megawatt-hour.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Operation Economic Outcast, an “unprecedented” sanctions campaign targeting Iran’s aviation, shipping, gold, technology, and digital asset sectors.
“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent told reporters.
He warned that any entity facilitating money laundering for Tehran would be permanently removed from the US dollar system and signaled that a major financial institution could be sanctioned by the end of the week.
The measures follow US President Donald Trump’s warning last week that Washington could sanction countries continuing to trade with Tehran.
Iran rejected the threats as a sign of desperation and argued that further sanctions would fail to force the country into submission.
European gas markets remain particularly vulnerable to developments in the Middle East, as tensions have kept the Strait of Hormuz largely closed and delayed Qatari liquefied natural gas shipments to Europe.
The disruption has coincided with stronger cooling demand during the summer heatwave, slowing the pace at which European countries are replenishing inventories.
The combination has raised pressure on storage levels and heightened concerns about whether Europe will enter the winter heating season with an adequate supply buffer.

Trump’s approval holds at record low as US support for Iran war falls, Reuters Ipsos poll finds
- US public support for military action against Iran has dropped to 31%, the lowest since the conflict began, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.
- President Donald Trump’s approval rating remains at a record low of 33%, influenced by declining backing for the war among Republicans.
- Most Americans (83%) believe the war will continue for a long time, showing increased concern about the conflict’s duration.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - US public approval of the war with Iran fell to its lowest level since the conflict’s early days, helping to hold President Donald Trump’s popularity at a record low, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Aug 24.
The four-day poll showed just 31 per cent of Americans support US military action against Iran, down from 37 per cent in a March Reuters/Ipsos poll and 34 per cent earlier this month.
The decline was driven by fewer self-identified Republicans backing the conflict. Some 69 per cent of Republican respondents support the war, compared with 77 per cent in March.
The war has been dragging on Trump’s public standing this year, and for the second survey in a row just 33 per cent of respondents said they approved of the Republican’s performance in the White House, the lowest level in polls from Trump’s first or second term.
Some 83 per cent of the country thinks the war will go on “for an extended period of time”, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found, up from 80 per cent earlier this month.
The poll surveyed 1,215 US adults nationwide and had a margin of error of 3 percentage points in either direction. REUTERS

German prosecutors identify likely suspect in deadly 1970 Munich Jewish center arson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:07:55 UTC
04:07:55 KST

The Munich Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office has closed the case involving an until-now-unsolved antisemitic arson attack on a Jewish community center after 56 years.
This was confirmed to The Jerusalem Post by the Munich Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Munich Police Headquarters on Monday.
On the evening of 13 February 1970, the building of the Jewish Community of Munich at 27 Reichenbachstraße in Munich, which was also a retirement home, was set alight using a petrol mixture.
Seven Jewish residents, survivors of the Holocaust, died as a result of the arson attack. A further 15 people were injured, four of them seriously.
Following a new tip-off from the public, the Munich Public Prosecutor’s Office reopened the investigation in April 2025, after the Federal Public Prosecutor had previously closed the case in 2017.
A witness provided the prosecutor with credible information about the suspect. According to this information, the suspect had been in close contact with one of her relatives in the 1970s. The suspect then died in 2020.
Shortly after this relative’s death, the informant revealed what she knew about the matter.
In order to verify the suspicion, investigators from the Munich Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office and the State Security Division of the Munich Police Headquarters examined the archived files of the Munich I Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office, and interviewed witnesses from the suspect’s circle.
According to the findings of the new investigations, the prosecutor said there are compelling grounds for believing that the (deceased) suspect was the perpetrator.
Investigators link deceased suspect to far-right circles
At the time, the suspect was a 25-year-old German man. On the evening of 13 February 1970, he is said to have remarked, in the immediate vicinity of the crime scene and with a view of the Jewish retirement home, that ‘the Jews have everything’ and that he wanted to ‘set them on fire’.
About 15 minutes later, the building was engulfed in flames. This information is based on the credible statement of the informant, who in turn was repeating the remarks made by her deceased relative. Other family members confirm these remarks.
The prosecutor subsequently found that the suspect was linked to far-right circles. Witnesses described him as an antisemite with a ‘Hitler obsession’. In his youth, he is said to have listened to Hitler’s speeches on records and practiced shooting in the former ‘Führer’s restricted area at Obersalzberg’.
A former schoolmate described the suspect’s hostility towards Jews as a defining characteristic.
A headteacher highlighted what they said was "a coldly calculating, attention-seeking manner" and reported a physical altercation during which the suspect is alleged to have used a dagger given to him by his father, which had belonged to the Hitler Youth.
Furthermore, the offender profile drawn up by the Bavarian Operational Case Analysis Unit on behalf of the Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office matches the deceased suspect. Overall, the prosecutor said the new investigations strongly suggest that the suspect was responsible.
Death of suspect leaves case without prosecution
However, it is not possible to reach a definitive legal conclusion, because prosecution is not legally possible in Germany against defendants who have already died.
Nevertheless, the investigation has not revealed any reliable evidence of the involvement of other individuals, and as such the Munich Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office has closed the investigation.

AI-generated music to be banned from ARIA charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:07:55 UTC
04:07:55 KST

In short:
Australia's main music charts have announced a ban on AI-generated music to start this week.
The Australian Recording Industry Association says wholly AI-generated tracks will not be eligible for the ARIA Charts, though recordings using AI in a supporting role will remain eligible.
It comes after a song produced with AI became the most-played track on Australian radio and reached number four on two ARIA charts in July.
Songs created mostly or entirely by artificial intelligence will be excluded from Australia's official music charts from this Friday, under new rules set down by the recording industry.
However, AI-assisted recordings can still chart if they are substantially human made.
The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA), which runs the charts of the most popular music in Australia, has updated its Charts Code of Practice to put it in line with principles put out by the global recording industry.
The updated code excludes music that has used generative AI unless it is "substantially human-made" and "raises no stream or chart manipulation concerns".
The new code lets ARIA remove ineligible recordings, alter chart positions and revoke chart awards. Artists and representatives can contest exclusions.
The change will apply to the charts released on Friday.
ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said while artists were already using AI tools, music generated wholly by services built on artists' recordings was a different matter altogether.
"This gives everyone who releases music in Australia a clear rule to work to," she said.
"We call on all parties who have a role in deciding the music played and promoted to Australian audiences, particularly radio, to support human artistry and implement similar changes across their own codes."
AI-generated music storming up the charts
The decision follows scrutiny of Queensland DJ and producer Josh Fawaz's cover of Madonna's Like a Prayer, which became the most-played song on Australian radio and reached number four on two ARIA charts in July.
The track attracted criticism from music figures who believed generative AI had been used.
Fawaz said he used AI "as a tool" and later updated the track listing on Spotify to say the vocals and drums were AI-generated.
ARIA's move draws from the principles published in July by the global body representing the recorded music industry, which said more than 20 official chart programs were adopting rules intended to distinguish human-created recordings from wholly AI-generated material.
An ARIA spokesperson told the ABC that the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) rules would likely disqualify music with lead vocals or key instrumentals are AI generated, suggesting Fawaz's song may not qualify under the new rules.
IFPI said its concerns included AI models trained on artists' music without authorisation from rights holders.
Loading...
Spotify has taken a different transparency measure when it comes to AI music.
It has pledged to badge AI personas and exclude them from recommendations by default, however that badge applies to just the identity behind an artist profile, not whether AI was used to make a particular recording.
ARIA's move comes amid a wider dispute between creative industries and AI companies, many of which have built their technology using copyrighted material without artists' permission.
The federal government is working on new rules for AI and data centres that would include "strong copyright protections for Australian creators".

Israel is using Qusra to show Palestinians the price of staying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:06:52 UTC
04:06:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel is using Qusra to show Palestinians the price of staying
For more than two weeks now, the Palestinian town of Qusra has been under an Israeli-imposed siege as the displacement of Palestinian families there persists. What began with Israeli settlers armed with military-issued weapons transformed into a joint military-settler operation.
At the beginning of the attack and siege, Israeli settlers had cut off water and electricity from the Palestinian residents in the town, with the purpose of driving them out and taking over their homes and lands. After some media attention and international recognition of the depravity happening in Qusra, the Israeli army moved in in lieu of the settlers, declaring the area a closed military zone and imposing their own restrictions. But in reality, this distinction between the army and settlers obscures what is happening in Qusra and in the West Bank generally.
They may wear different clothes, but in the end what is happening is that armed Israelis are imposing the same political reality, one where Palestinians cannot exist or live freely in their own homes.
What Qusra does offer us is not another story of settler impunity, but a clear showcasing of how dispossession can happen through the division of labour.
The siege: different forms of enclosures
When we speak of a siege, there may be a tendency to imagine something with a perimeter. A barricade, soldiers surrounding the city, tanks stationed at entrances and exits, and darkness as a population is completely cut off from the outside world. Yet what we see in the West Bank is a much more dispersed form of enclosures.
Over the last couple of years, the West Bank has witnessed record-high restrictions on movement affecting all 3.4 million Palestinians. As of December 2025, there is a 43% annual increase in movement obstacles affecting Palestinians. The Israeli security apparatus, in coordination with Israeli settlers, has erected gates at the entrances and exits of every Palestinian town and village, designated dozens of roads as forbidden to Palestinians, hoisted hundreds of military-controlled checkpoints, declared dozens of acres as closed military zones, approved dozens of new outposts, and reclassified Palestinian lands as Israel.
What this has done is make movement conditional. The enclosures do not have to be continuous to be effective. What they have meant for daily calculations is that Palestinians may leave their homes, but not go through that road (and instead endure an hours-long detour with the possibility of being stopped and beaten at a checkpoint), that they may reach their farmlands, but not this week.
It means they may go to work and school, but at risk of being attacked by armed Israelis who have decided to gather at a major roundabout. In the case of Qusra, it means you may remain in your home, but someone could come and make remaining there progressively impossible.
Looking at these dynamics, it becomes clearer that the West Bank is a large open-air prison. One which may not operate as a conventional prison but as a prison whose walls can move, randomly and repeatedly.
This is perhaps the most striking aspect of highlighting Qusra without context. It inadvertently suggests that this besiegement of families across three homes is an aberration in an otherwise functioning territory.
The shrinking distance between home and frontier
The case of Qusra should emphasise and magnify to the world exactly what Palestinians encounter across the West Bank, and that is a relentlessly shrinking distinction between home and frontier. This has been Israel’s strategy of anticipation where it engineers the expectation of expulsion, and is even using Qusra as an instrument to punctuate this reality.
What is being said, through this organised state violence, is that any Palestinian home or land can become a target. If it is not taken over by Israeli settlers, it is declared a military zone and taken by the army, and at best it becomes a case of “contested land,” which can protract for weeks, months, or even years.
What we see is not a simple act of controlling territory, but a new geography of occupation where it becomes about altering the conditions of reality under which Palestinians can inhabit these lands. So, rather than expel an entire village and obliterate entire cities as was the case in Gaza, Israel is teaching Palestinians what staying will cost.
Right now, what Israel is doing in Qusra and elsewhere in the West Bank does not stop at displacement. It is forcing Palestinians to consider: “Is this house still worth living in?” “Can my children safely grow up here?” “If I leave for work this morning, will I be able to return in the evening?”
Qusra exposes an architecture of colonialism in which the West Bank is experienced as one large enclosure without the need for a wall. While Gaza has made the word “siege” synonymous with a territory encircled from the outside, Qusra and the West Bank require that we recognise another form of siege. One which advances from the inside of the territory where the perimeter is constantly redrawn around Palestinian lives.
We must understand that Qusra is not an isolated incident of settlers and military between settlers and three families. It is three families against one of the strongest and most brutal regimes of our time, and it doesn’t end with them. It extends to all Palestinians in the West Bank facing a large-scale transformation which not only seizes lands and homes, but holds captive Palestinian lives.
The world needs to move not just for Qusra, but for Palestinians and what remains of Palestinian lives and will to persist. The walls of this prison do not stand still; they move around us, compressing spaces in which life can be ordinary, where even our own homes become Israel’s battlefields.
Displacement and dispossession are not sudden events of violent expulsion; they are the acts of siege that happen in Palestinian daily life.
Mariam Barghouti is a writer and journalist based in the West Bank. She has been covering the region as a reporter and analyst for ten years, served as the senior Palestine correspondent for Mondoweiss, and is a member of the Marie Colvin Journalist Network.
