As Russian drone incursions escalate, NATO weighs costs of shooting back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
19:04:11 UTC
04:04:11 KST

As Russian drone incursions escalate, NATO weighs costs of shooting back
F-16 fighter jets from the Turkish Air Force fly over Canakkale, Turkiye, on May 11, 2026. (Ali Atmaca / Anadolu via Getty Images)
For years, NATO countries have watched Russian drones breach their airspace, reluctant to shoot them down for fear of escalation. That restraint is now beginning to erode.
After Russian drones killed civilians in Romania, while Russian electronic jamming continued diverting Ukrainian drones toward critical infrastructure in the Baltic region, NATO fighter jets finally began shooting intruders down.
But using expensive air-to-air missiles to destroy cheap, one-way Geran and Gerbera drones is hardly a sustainable solution. Europe, therefore, faces a pressing challenge: building a new, cost-effective drone shield capable of protecting its eastern flank from persistent Russian incursions.
Turning that ambition into reality, however, will be far from easy.
European capitals will need to overcome significant technological hurdles, improve coordination across borders and military services, and — perhaps most importantly — demonstrate the political will to invest in a defensive architecture designed for a threat that is already evolving faster than traditional air-defense systems.
Drones test NATO's frontier
Since 2023, Russian drones have been crashing on the Romanian side of the Danube River border during Moscow's attacks against Ukrainian ports. Moldova, a non-NATO neighbor of Romania and Ukraine, has also come under fire.
Further north, drones and missiles have repeatedly strayed into Polish airspace — but it was only in September 2025 when, for the first time, allied jets downed four of about 20 Russian drones in an unprecedented incursion.
In December that year, Turkey downed a drone approaching its airspace across the Black Sea — a key battlefield for both aerial and naval drones.
After a Russian drone struck a residential building and injured two civilians in the Romanian city of Galati on May 29, Bucharest hardened its response as well.
A Romanian F-16 shot down a Shahed-type drone on July 24, with three more drones downed in the following weeks.
Only in the first half of the year did Romanian authorities record over 40 incursions, and more are reported every week — most recently when Romanian jets destroyed a suspected Russian naval drone near the Black Sea gas project Neptun Deep on Aug. 20.
Western officials suspect at least some incursions to be intentional provocations, while other drones have likely simply veered off course by mistake or after being hit by Ukrainian defenses.
And NATO's northeastern flank has also felt the impact of the drone war as Russian jamming and spoofing increasingly diverts Ukrainian strike drones — targeting Russian ports and refineries — into the Baltic and Finland.
The first downing of a drone by a NATO jet over Estonia took place on May 19, and two were downed over Latvia on June 8 and Aug. 14.
Europe's drone wall(s)
The incursions have spurred a cascade of national and transnational initiatives meant to reinforce Europe's response.
While NATO's Eastern Sentry strengthens the flank with existing hardware like fighter jets, the EU's European Drone Defense Initiative (EDDI) — often dubbed the "Drone Wall" — aims to roll out a multi-layered defense of radars, jammers, and advanced interceptors tailored more specifically to counter unmanned systems.
On top of that, Poland is developing a new dedicated anti-drone system as part of its Eastern Shield project, while also participating in the "Baltic Drone Wall" initiative alongside Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia.
The task at hand is not only to secure the skies, but to do so in a cost-effective way.
If an F-16 fires an AIM-9X Sidewinder missile against a Shahed drone, it applies a $400,000 solution to a $35,000 problem. And that price tag does not include other costs of operating the plane.
One Ukraine-tested answer is interceptor drones.
In November 2025, Poland announced it had received its first U.S.-designed Merops: light, AI-driven systems that launch Surveyor interceptor drones worth around $15,000.
The system has been praised for its performance on Ukrainian battlefields, with U.S. Army Brigadier General Curtis King saying Merops was responsible for about 40% of Shahed drone interceptions.
Romania first tested the system in April, while Lithuania is rushing to buy its first test batch of 48 Surveyor drones through a fast-tracked procurement procedure.
Others turn to homegrown solutions, with the Baltic Drone Wall integrating Latvia's Blaze interceptor drones with Estonia's Eirshield drone platform.
Anti-aircraft cannons, cheaper missiles, and electronic warfare systems are also on the shopping lists of NATO countries.
Romania is buying 24 Skyranger systems and seven Skynex systems under a 5.7 billion-euro ($6.6 billion) contract with Rheinmetall, in addition to six Israeli short- and medium-range Spyder missile launchers.
Meanwhile, Polish defense companies, in collaboration with Norway's Kongsberg, have unveiled what is vaunted as Europe's largest and most complex counter-drone system — SAN.
Announced as part of the Polish Eastern Shield, SAN is set to field 18 counter-drone batteries in layered defenses encompassing 30 mm anti-air guns, interceptor drones, and guided APKWS rockets.
Why jets are not going anywhere
Yet all the recent interceptions were handled by fighter jets rather than by the new counter-drone systems.
Part of the reason is simple timing.
SAN is expected to start operations only in late 2026; the European Drone Wall should be fully functional next year, and Romania's larger batteries will start arriving only by the end of the decade.
And the cost of taking down the drone is not the only factor in the calculation.
The cost of an air-to-air missile is ultimately small compared with the potential human and economic toll of allowing a drone to get through and cause casualties or damage critical infrastructure, according to Federico Borsari, a security expert at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA).
For Ukraine, intercepting hundreds of drones on an almost daily basis has become part of the reality of war. Even with extensive air defenses, some drones are inevitably going to get through.
A country at peace is likely to view the risk differently. A single drone killing a civilian or striking critical infrastructure such as a power plant can have an outsized impact, making governments more inclined to use the most reliable interception methods available — even when they are considerably more expensive.
Furthermore, "asset availability, operational conditions, and the type of target also play a role" when responding to an incursion, Borsari adds.
Justin Bronk, an air power expert at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) think tank, notes that dispatching fighters to stop individual drones is simpler than tackling the "huge personnel and logistics requirements of fielding thousands of individually cheap short-range systems like Merops" across the whole border.
Experts agree that fighter jets remain an important part of counter-drone infrastructure. The focus, Bronk notes, should be on acquiring cheaper munitions for them, "such as APKWS II and Thales laser-guided rockets."
Gaps to overcome
While the number of new counter-drone initiatives is impressive, some analysts warn of pitfalls.
Ulrike Franke, a researcher at the European Council on Foreign Relations, writes that this "hotch-potch" of projects may disperse focus and lead to duplication of efforts.
The EU should rein in its ambitions for the Drone Wall to "do just about everything" and focus on the most successful national initiatives in Poland and the Baltics, Franke argues. The bloc, she writes, should also prod other frontier states to step up.
Both she and Borsari see interoperability among individual allies and industry players as a key obstacle to overcome.
And while Borsari lists other weaknesses — such as insufficient training, experimentation, and, in some cases, funding — he acknowledges progress.
The EU is opening the tap for drone investment, with its 150-billion-euro ($175-billion) SAFE loans helping fund air defense acquisitions in Poland and Romania.
The NATO summit in Ankara, in turn, saw allies pledge to invest $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities over the next five years.
Since spring 2026, the alliance has been holding regular LCI-X Crucible exercises focused on countering drones, with Ukrainian soldiers participating.
"I expect (counter-drone) capabilities across the alliance to improve significantly in the near future, though for some areas, especially training and full operational capability… may require time," Borsari predicts.
Finding the will
Barring physical constraints, countering drone incursions is still hitting political obstacles.
Only last May did Romania adopt a law authorizing its military to shoot down drones and aircraft that violate its airspace in peacetime.
Lithuania's parliament adopted similar legislation in September, a few weeks after the incursion into Poland.
And there is still the question of the readiness to pull the trigger.
The obstacles here are two-fold, says Iulian Chifu, a Romanian security analyst and president of the Center for Conflict Prevention & Early Warning, a research institute in Bucharest.
Firstly, the allies worry that the downing — or an attempt at it— may cause more collateral damage than if the intruding drone is allowed to leave the airspace or crash in an empty area.
Secondly, many fear that opening fire will bring Russia to view European countries as co-belligerents — an idea Moscow "succeeded in putting into the heads of European leaders," Chifu adds.
But the recent incidents seem to be changing the risk calculus for European nations.
In Romania, the breaking point was when the Russian drone hit the residential building, according to Chifu.
And in Latvia, a crash of stray Ukrainian drones at a local oil facility in May led to the fall of the Latvian government.
The political cost of letting the drones slip through may begin to outweigh the cost of shooting them down.

UK Power Networks, which operates the electricity network across south-east England, had to isolate an overhead power cable while crews worked below.
A spokesperson for West Sussex fire and rescue service said: “Approximately 140 vehicles were damaged, and a number of the vehicles involved in this fire were parked at a site used for holiday parking. Any affected consumers are advised to contact their operator directly.”
There were no casualties, it said.
The fire also caused significant damage to two breakdown and recovery businesses and a banger racing team.
The Bears banger racing team said in a fundraiser that they had lost everything.
Autocovery and K&L Automotive had also previously donated abandoned vehicles to fire stations across West Sussex for training purposes, according to local reports.
Sussex police said a 67-year-old man arrested on suspicion of arson had been bailed pending further inquiries.
“Power was shut off to the immediate area, affecting a number of businesses and homes, and nearby roads were closed as a precaution,” a spokesperson said.
“Emergency services remain on scene at this time and the public are advised to avoid the area.”
A London Gatwick spokesperson said: “We are aware of a fire at an unaffiliated third-party car parking site, which occurred on Saturday evening, and understand how concerning and distressing this will be for any passengers whose vehicles may have been affected.
“We are advising any passengers who are concerned that their vehicle might have been affected to contact their parking operator directly.
“The parking company is not endorsed or operated by London Gatwick.”
Police said anyone with information about the incident was asked to report it online or call 101, quoting serial number 1504.

Vance claims Canada is reliant on US defence umbrella to deter foreign invasion
Unknown

2026-08-24
19:00:02 UTC
04:00:02 KST

US Vice President JD Vance has said that Canada has failed to invest in its military and would be invaded by another country without the protection provided by the United States.
"Canada is a country that has underinvested in its military that quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America," Vance told an audience on Monday in Brewer, Maine, a northern state bordering Canada.
Vance also criticised Canada over recent trade tensions with the US, accusing Ottawa of making unreasonable demands during negotiations.
"They came in with a bunch of unreasonable last-minute demands," Vance said.
"I think that we should have a deal, but I think that we need to send a message loud and clear to the prime minister of Canada: stop taking advantage of the people of Maine. Stop taking advantage of America. It’s over. We expect fairness in our trade policy."
His remarks come as President Donald Trump has repeatedly pressed Canada and other US allies to increase defence spending while seeking more favorable trade terms.
Trump has imposed tariffs on Canadian goods and repeatedly criticised Ottawa over trade practices, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has sought to negotiate with Washington to ease tensions between the two neighbours.
Canada is a member of both NATO and NORAD, a joint US-Canadian organisation responsible for monitoring and defending the airspace and maritime approaches of North America.
Ottawa has pledged to increase defence spending as geopolitical tensions grow, including amid Russia's war in Ukraine and rising strategic competition in the Arctic.
Trade talks collapse
The comments came as trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa escalated further. New US tariffs of 50 percent on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods took effect on Saturday after trade talks collapsed.
Trump on Monday threatened an additional 50 percent tariff on Canadian automobiles, auto parts, and steel starting on January 1, 2027. Canada has vowed to retaliate.
Earlier on Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent during a press conference in Washington DC was asked if President Trump is still interested in making Canada the 51st US state.
"I think he would like Canada to come to the table and negotiate in good faith. They were offered quite a good deal last week. They chose to reject it," Bessent answered.
He accused Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney of rising to power on an "anti-American, anti-Trump platform", and questioned why Carney, a former Bank of Canada governor, would reject the deal if he truly has the Canadian people's interests at heart.
Carney said on Monday that the goal of trade talks with Washington "has always been to get the best deal for Canadians, never a deal at any price or on any time frame."
"We learned that, during the negotiations, the Americans wanted to destroy our major industries — including the automotive, steel, and aluminum sectors — through unfair negotiating terms. And that is one of the main reasons why we said no," he added.
He stressed that building domestically and diversifying trade abroad has been "plan A from the start."
Canadian officials also said that trade talks with the US collapsed after Washington sought to impose restrictions on Ottawa regarding trade deals with other countries.

The San Francisco 49ers had not immediately issued a statement on the case.
York has been with the 49ers organization since 2008 and served as the team's CEO for many years. He became the franchise's principal owner in 2024.
During York's tenure, the 49ers have reached three Super Bowls and seven NFC Championship Games.
The arrest came less than three weeks before the start of the 2026 National Football League regular season, with the 49ers scheduled to open their campaign against the Los Angeles Rams on Sept. 10.

The FSB initially ordered her to provide information on artists and political activists both within and outside of Russia and took her passport so she couldn't leave the country. According to Flores, they reportedly wanted her to help develop some into fellow "assets" and to help line up new targets for criminal cases.
In an Instagram post, Flores described those three years as being defined by "prolonged depression... complete, unrelenting derealization, PTSD from being followed and surveilled... several attempts at suicide, and so, so, so much more."
The pressure from the FSB ramped up when they tried to force her to help lure Mediazona co-founder and activist Pyotr Verzilov to Serbia so they could murder him.
According to Flores, she contacted lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov afterward and managed to stall the FSB's demands until she was finally able to escape Russia.
The Kyiv Independent reached out to Verzilov after the revelation.
"The FSB has been trying to kill me for the last 10 years in various parts of the world," Verzilov said.
"Their repeated attempts in the last several years are a testament of the work we do, first of all of the work focused on the defense of Ukraine in the face of Russian aggression."
Without providing details of her escape, Flores thanked Zakhvatov and businessman Leonid Nevzlin for being among those who helped her leave the country.
She did not disclose where she is currently located, only that she went public to offer hope to those in the same situation.

Donald Trump announced a new 50% tariff on automobiles and crucial raw materials from Canada, the latest deterioration in trade relations between the two neighbors with historically strong economic ties.
The US president said that the increased tariffs would start on 1 January 2027 on all cars, trucks, automobile parts and steel. He also derided the nation’s tariffs on American farmers, writing on social media that Canada has been “ripping off” the US “for years”.
“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” he wrote on Truth Social. “They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!”
In response, Mark Carney told reporters on Monday that Trump’s announcement was largely expected.
“It’s not a surprise for us that the US would take some form of reprisal to our response to their unjustified tariff, which was on top of other unjustified tariffs,” the Canadian prime minister said from Quebec.
“But what message does that send to the workers in Michigan, in Ohio, in Kentucky, in Alabama, who rely on Canadian demand?” Carney continued. “We’re their largest customer for automobiles, more than the European Union, Japan, Korea, many others combined, and the United Kingdom.”
He added that Canada would be ready to move forward with talks “when the Americans go to the negotiating table first with the right attitude toward our industry and a true partnership”.
Trump’s announcement follows the last-minute collapse this weekend of a potential deal to lower tariffs on automobiles and other materials. After Trump imposed another 50% tariff on $20bn worth of Canadian exports, including hockey equipment and electronics, Carney, rejected the latest deal between the two nations on Saturday.
Carney said that the US “asked too much and they offered too little”, and he has vowed to match the American tariffs “dollar for dollar”.
Canada and the US have been longtime partners, trading roughly $909bn, according to the office of the US trade representative. But Trump’s second presidential term and his aggressive trade policies have brought the era of “deep ties” between the two nations to a close, Carney said last year, vowing to fight Trump’s sweeping tariffs.

Ex-Pussy Riot member Rita Flores says she cooperated with the FSB for nearly three years before escaping Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:53:11 UTC
03:53:11 KST

Former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores has stated that in February 2023, officers from the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) coerced her into cooperating with them by using threats of criminal prosecution and physical violence against her and her loved ones. According to Flores, in the years that followed she passed information about artists and political activists to the security service. Then, in the summer of 2025, she received an assignment to help organize the killing of former Mediazona publisher and Pussy Riot member Pyotr Verzilov.
Flores recounted the story in an interview with lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov, who had helped her flee Russia around ten days earlier. In a conversation with The Insider, Zakhvatov said that he learned of Flores’s relationship with the security services in the summer of 2005, and preparations for her evacuation had taken roughly a year.
How the FSB recruited Flores
According to Flores, she was recruited on Feb. 17, 2023, following a search of her Moscow apartment. That day, media reported that her phone and laptop had been seized and a message had been sent from her phone to her lawyer stating that she had been taken to the Investigative Committee. Flores now says that in reality she had remained at home with two FSB officers.
Zakhvatov told The Insider that the recruitment was preceded by prolonged psychological pressure: Flores had been detained multiple times, placed in temporary detention centers, subjected to surveillance, and had her home searched. According to the lawyer, the final search differed from the previous iterations. This time, one of the officers who entered the apartment addressed Flores in a markedly gentle tone before his colleague began applying intense pressure on her.
“First they worked her over psychologically like that, then threatened her into signing one document, then two days later they made her sign another,” Zakhvatov told The Insider.
As the lawyer stresses, Flores already had extensive experience dealing with the security forces. She had taken part in Pussy Riot protests and was detained multiple times. She knew she was being watched, and Zakhvatov himself had previously helped her evade surveillance.
“It’s difficult to say she was completely unprepared. Nevertheless, under certain circumstances, if you find the right approach to a person and hit a vulnerable spot, then, as practice has shown, [recruitment] is possible,” he said.
“Harley”: tracking artists and activists for the FSB
Flores herself recounted that during the process, the officers threatened her with criminal charges over posts she had made about Russian soldiers killing civilians in Bucha, and the officers also made threats about her family members. She was later taken to the security service’s building on Michurinsky Avenue, where she signed cooperation documents. According to Flores, she was given the operational alias “Harley” and was assigned a handler — an FSB officer named Ivan.
Flores’s first assignment, she says, was to compile profiles on contemporary artists from Russia and neighboring countries. She was subsequently required to gather information on potential law enforcement targets, including details about their associates, relatives, habits, and vulnerabilities including drug use, infidelities, and mental health. According to Flores, this data could be used as tools of pressure and blackmail.
Flores claims she tried to sabotage her work by withholding information that could be dangerous to people she knew, and she deliberately cut off contact with individuals whom the FSB assigned her to “develop.” At the same time, according to her, the security service gained access to her phone through surveillance software.
Zakhvatov told The Insider that Flores had indeed tried to avoid carrying out her assignments.
“She tried to wriggle out of things in every way she could. Sometimes it worked, sometimes it didn’t. But fortunately, no one was harmed,” the lawyer said.
Among those she was required to gather information on, Flores named street artist Phillip Kozlov, known as Philippenzo, who in the summer of 2023 created graffiti titled “Izrossilovanie” (a fusion of the words “Russia” and “rape”). Kozlov was later detained, received two consecutive 15-day administrative sentences, and became a subject in a criminal vandalism case. He subsequently left Russia.
The plot to kill Pyotr Verzilov
The most serious assignment, Flores claims, came in the summer of 2025. According to her, FSB officers proposed that she help organize the killing of Pyotr Verzilov, the unofficial spokesperson of Pussy Riot, with whom she had previously been in a relationship. Flores was to lure him to Serbia and arrange a meeting at a predetermined café.
“After that, I was supposed to step outside on some pretext,” Flores said. According to her, the plan was to then abduct and kill Verzilov.
For her participation in the operation, she was allegedly offered a reward of up to 3 million rubles ($36,000). Flores also claims that her handlers repeatedly asked her to find at least a partial image of Verzilov’s house in Ukraine in order to establish his location and place an explosive device nearby.
After receiving the assignment related to Verzilov, Flores reached out to Zakhvatov. They then began working on extricating her from the security service’s control and arranging her departure from Russia.
The lesson for other coerced informants
According to Zakhvatov, one of the key tasks was to recover Flores’s passport. They also initially considered a course of action in which the activist would pretend to agree to take part in the killing of Verzilov in order to create the opportunity for arresting the FSB team on Serbian territory, but the idea was ultimately abandoned.
“It was too dangerous for Rita. And most importantly, the plan lacked credibility. The FSB officers knew very well that Rita and Pyotr had been close. We thought that such a proposal might itself be a provocation on their part, or could trigger a serious loyalty test for Rita, which she most likely would have failed,” Zakhvatov explained.
After that, they focused on preparing the evacuation. The lawyer has declined to disclose how Flores managed to leave Russia.
Flores noted that she received money from the Russian security services in exchange for her cooperation. Initially she was given a one-time payment of 30,000 rubles ($360), and in the final months before her departure, she says, the FSB paid her 50,000 rubles ($600) per month.
Following Flores’s evacuation, Zakhvatov published an appeal to others who may have been recruited by Russian intelligence services and wish to stop cooperating. As the lawyer explained to The Insider, this is not a dedicated evacuation program for informants, so he does not expect a large number of such inquiries. However, according to him, the Flores case has demonstrated the need to create a dedicated communication channel for people in a similar predicament.
“Since this situation has arisen, we need to use it somehow to disrupt the recruiters’ game... If a person has encountered the same problem as Rita did, they can reach out and receive some form of assistance,” Zakhvatov told The Insider.
He left separate contact details for such inquiries on Element X, Telegram, and Proton email while urging people not to contact him from devices known to the Russian security services.
According to Zakhvatov, one of the most important things an informant who has reached safety must do is speak openly about their cooperation with the security service. Keeping this fact secret, the lawyer argues, allows recruiters to continue using it as leverage and compel a person to carry out assignments even after leaving Russia.
“You’ve already been hooked, you’ve already been reeled in, some trace has already been left. That trace means that at any moment — as the recruitment victim understands — you can be held accountable for it and can be forced to do things you don’t want to do... It’s important that people don’t stay silent,” Zakhvatov told The Insider.
According to the lawyer, this is precisely why it was important to make Flores’s full story public — detailing the methods that FSB officers allegedly used on her.
“People need to know about all these methods; they need to be publicized so that people understand how to handle such a situation correctly and avoid falling into this trap,” he said.
Flores herself also explained her decision to publicly disclose her FSB cooperation as coming from a desire to help others in similar situations.
“I suspect more people have been recruited. And I would like to help them. I am a living example that you can simply reach out to the right people, and they will help you one hundred percent,” she said.

One is making his name in tackle football, the other in the soccer version: Meet the Flowers
EUGENE, Ore. (AP) — Football is a family affair for the Flowers brothers. They just differ on the definition.
Aaron Flowers plays American football for No. 2 Oregon, while younger brother Benji was developed by the vaunted FC Dallas soccer academy and just signed a deal with Chelsea.
Benji, now 15, will join the Premier League team when he turns 18. Until then, he’ll continue to work on his game in Texas. He became the youngest player to sign a professional contract with the senior team as a homegrown player in late July.
Benji jokes that he wasn’t cut out for his big brother’s brand of football.
“Well, he was way bigger than me, and also I think that he could take hits more, way more than me, and he was like twice my weight, twice my height, like around my age. So I think that’s probably why my parents thought it was like really dangerous for me,” Benji Flowers said. ”So they put him in it, and they told me to stick with soccer.”
Aaron, meanwhile, ultimately chose the other football. A four-star safety out of Forney, Texas, where the brothers grew up, Aaron went with Oregon over USC, Baylor, Oklahoma, Arkansas and Alabama.
“So I played soccer as well growing up when I was younger. But then I got bigger and I was too physical and getting red cards. So I stopped playing,” Aaron said. “But my little brother, I mean, he played soccer. He wasn’t as big as I was, obviously, he was shorter. So then my parents were too scared to put him in football, and he just blossomed and then became really good at soccer.”
Benji begins making his mark on the pitch
With the Dallas academy since he was 10, Benji made his debut with Dallas’ MLS Next Pro team, North Texas SC, this year. The Dallas academy has previously produced such U.S. stars as Ricardo Pepi and Weston McKennie, who were both on the roster for this summer’s World Cup.
Benji Flowers knew he wanted to make soccer a career well before he joined the academy.
“When I first started playing, at that point I was just playing for fun, and then around the age of like, I’ll say 6 is when I made my dream that I want to be pro, and I want to make this my living,” he said. “So, yeah, that’s when I really started taking stuff seriously.”
Chelsea’s fee for Benji is a reported $3 million, but add-ons could take it to $10 million.
MLS Commissioner Don Garber told The Associated Press that the contract with Chelsea shows the league’s push to build up its academy system is paying off.
“It’s probably the single-biggest validation of our player-development programs in recent memory, and I’m really excited about it, and I’m proud of it because we’ve been working for a long time and spending enormous resources in improving the player-development programs at our clubs,” Garber said.
Flowers is also a prospect for the U.S. national team. He has played for the U.S. under-15 team and has scored two goals in three appearances this year.
“Benji has embraced every step of that journey through hard work, determination and the support of his family,” FC Dallas President Dan Hunt said in a statement. “His signing is a reflection of the tremendous work being done throughout the FC Dallas Academy and reinforces what is possible for the next generation of players.
Aaron becomes a standout on the gridiron
Aaron, who also ran track in high school, utilized a redshirt after appearing in two games for Oregon during the 2024 season. He broke out in 2025, starting in all 15 games for the Ducks as they made a run to the national semifinals. He ranked third on Oregon’s defense with 70 total tackles, including 37 solo.
Last season, Aaron Flowers was paired with safety Dillon Thieneman, now with the Chicago Bears. This season, he’ll likely start in tandem with Koi Perich, a transfer from Minnesota.
Oregon went 13-2 last season, with the losses coming to Fernando Mendoza-led Indiana — once in the regular season then again in a College Football Playoff semifinal.
Aaron said he’s sure Benji will be watching the Ducks, who aspire to reach the playoffs again, from afar. And of course, as a proud older brother, he’ll be following Benji’s career.
“I already knew he was really good,” Flowers said. “When I came back home, he scored five goals in one game. I was like, ‘Oh yeah, this dude’s going pro.’ And then just seeing it happen just really made me proud, and just happy to see that for him.”

Turkey sentences 5 opposition mayors in cases critics slam as politically motivated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

Turkey sentences 5 opposition mayors in cases critics slam as politically motivated
ISTANBUL (AP) — A Turkish court on Monday convicted five mayors of municipalities run by the country’s main opposition party on corruption charges in a trial that critics have denounced as politically motivated.
The case before an Istanbul court included allegations of bribery, bid-rigging and fraud in relation to municipal contracts. Critics of the government of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan say the trial targeted the opposition Republican People’s Party, or CHP, and that the prosecution relied on secret witnesses and defendants implicating other defendants in return for lighter punishment.
The Turkish government insists the country’s judiciary is independent and free from political influence.
The case focused on allegations that companies controlled by businessman Aziz Ihsan Aktas secured municipal tenders through bribery, bid-rigging and fraud. The opposition, meanwhile, has said that municipalities under Erdogan’s party control that did business with Aktas were not as thoroughly investigated.
Of the five convicted, the mayor of Istanbul’s Besiktas district, Riza Akpolat, received the heftiest sentence of 23 years and three months for accepting bribes, money laundering and bid-rigging.
The sentences of the four other mayors — who like Akpolat were removed from their posts following their arrests — ranged between five and eight years.
The seven-month trial in a courthouse next to Silivri Prison, west of Istanbul, included 200 defendants. Some of them were also sentenced while others were acquitted, though details of their cases were not immediately clear.
Aktas was arrested in Istanbul in January last year, after which authorities launched investigations into other Istanbul districts controlled by the Republican People’s Party, or CHP. The southern Turkish municipalities of Adana and Adiyaman, both run by CHP, were also investigated.
Aktas initially denied the charges but later testified against co-defendants under Turkey’s “effective repentance” law, alleging he had provided mayors and other officials with cash, cars and other bribes to get municipal contracts.
Aktas was separately tried and sentenced to two years and eight months for bid-rigging but was acquitted of bribery charges.
Most of the defendants denied knowing Aktas and accused him of giving false evidence. They also said that tenders had been allocated under long-standing processes and previous audits had uncovered no irregularities.
Another controversial aspect of the trial was the use of secret witnesses by the prosecution, many of whom admitted their evidence was based on hearsay.
Akpolat, the mayor of Besiktas, told the court that investigators offered to drop the charges if he gave evidence in a separate investigation into the CHP’s 2023 congress.
That investigation led to a court ordering the removal of the CHP’s top echelon in May on the grounds of voting irregularities during leadership elections. Many CHP members followed deposed leader Ozgur Ozel to the New Party, which is now the largest opposition group in parliament.
The CHP won several major cities in the 2019 local elections, including Istanbul and Ankara, the country’s capital. Further wins followed in the 2024 municipal polls but since then, an array of court cases have been brought against the opposition.
Ekrem Imamoglu, the metropolitan mayor of Istanbul and the opposition’s favored challenger to Erdogan in the next presidential election, has been behind bars since March last year.
He faces several legal cases, with the main one alleging corruption within the Istanbul municipality — claims that echo those in the Aktas case. If convicted, he could be sentenced to more than 2,300 years in total.

Darline Graham, Ralph Norman wrap up a whirlwind South Carolina Senate primary campaign
COLUMBIA, S.C. (AP) — Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman are wrapping up their compressed campaigns to win South Carolina’s Republican nomination in a special U.S. Senate primary to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham on November ballots.
Tuesday’s Senate runoff tests the heft of both a famous political last name and the endorsement of President Donald Trump, who is backing Darline Graham and campaigned in the state for her days ahead of the vote.
The matchup pits the well-known Norman — fresh off an unsuccessful gubernatorial bid earlier this summer — against Graham, the late senator’s sister who was thrust into the political spotlight with her interim appointment, then a sprint of a primary campaign.
Trump making final push for Darline Graham
Graham drew early criticism for being in Washington for Senate votes instead of on the ground in South Carolina, where many voters said they didn’t know anything about her or her positions. She’s been trying to make up that ground, holding meet and greet events, including two on Monday in Aiken and Seneca, as well as a news conference with Gov. Henry McMaster, who appointed her to the interim post and endorsed Graham on Friday.
Trump on Monday night also planned the second of two tele-rallies for Graham.
The president, long closely allied with Lindsey Graham, has done more to promote Darline Graham’s candidacy than he has for others he’s endorsed in this year’s midterms. Trump encouraged her to run and traveled to South Carolina on Friday for a rally with Graham in Myrtle Beach.
Before several thousand people — some of whom said they came mostly to see the president, not his chosen candidate — Trump urged “every South Carolina patriot to go to the polls and vote for Darline Graham.”
When McMaster appointed Graham last month, a person familiar with McMaster’s thinking but unauthorized to speak publicly about it said the governor had never contemplated that she would run for the seat herself.
Asked Monday why he had waited until late last week to endorse Graham, McMaster said simply that “I thought that was the right time.”
Norman crisscrossing the state to make his final campaign case
On Monday, Norman planned two events with pastors, ending his runoff campaign in Greenville. The most populous in the state, Greenville County typically contributes the most votes in statewide Republican primaries.
It’s also bucked against the front-runners in recent GOP contests. Norman also carried Greenville County in the gubernatorial primary earlier this year — and it was one of the only counties Lindsey Graham lost in his final election, this year’s original June primary.
Norman has decried the role of super PAC spending against him in the runoff campaign, accusing Graham of being funded by special interests who are pushing their own agenda through her candidacy. The wealthy developer has made large personal transfers into his campaign coffers and promoted his voting record and business acumen.
Norman has frequently reminded voters of his history supporting the president’s policies in Congress. He’s also portrayed his opponent as inexperienced for a six-year shot at the Senate job, saying in a wide-ranging interview with The Associated Press that the “Washington elite” who funded Graham were “dictating the terms and giving her the political answers” in her campaign.
At a town hall Friday, Norman leaned into his experience in elected politics and in the business world, reiterating his campaign trail slight against Graham, a political newcomer, that the Senate isn’t a place to get “training on the job.”
“We’ve had a short runway, and I’m so glad I did this,” Norman told voters at a town hall in Anderson. “You have to know it. You have to be in it, and that’s one of the advantages that I have.”
The winner of Tuesday’s GOP runoff will face Democrat Annie Andrews in November. No Democrat has won a statewide-elected office in South Carolina in two decades.

A psychologist at Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial says she has bipolar disorder
Unknown

A psychologist at Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial says she has bipolar disorder
Lindsay Clancy has bipolar disorder and was experiencing anxiety, depression, insomnia and suicidal thoughts in the weeks before she killed her three children, a forensic psychologist testified Monday in her murder trial
Kirk Heilbrun, who examined Clancy over three days this year, said he came to a different conclusion than a forensic psychiatrist who also evaluated her and testified Friday that Clancy neither had bipolar disorder nor psychosis.
Both Heilbrun and Dr. Avram Mack testified as rebuttal witnesses for prosecutors in a case that centers around Clancy’s mental state when she strangled her three young children before jumping from a second-story window in January 2023. Closing arguments are expected later this week.
___
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
___
Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington does not dispute that she killed the children. But he says she shouldn’t be held criminally responsible because she had postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth. He said she also had bipolar disorder and that antidepressants prescribed worsened her condition.
Prosecutors say the former labor and delivery nurse planned the killings and contrived to get her husband out of the house by sending him to pick up medicine for one of their children and dinner for the family.
Heilbrun said he struggled to reach a diagnosis of bipolar 2 disorder “because of all the diagnoses in the records and all the symptoms that she experienced.” People with bipolar 2 disorder experience cycles of depression and hypomania, which is less intense than the mania experienced with bipolar 1 disorder.
“I was having a hard time finding something that looked like it was a manic episode,” Heilbrun said. “There were times when she felt, as she described it, after the birth of different children, she felt good. She felt on top of the world. She felt really close to them, her husband and her kids and so on. But, it’s also something that it didn’t look like a manic episode so much as it looked like she was really feeling good.”
Heilbrun echoed earlier testimony about Clancy’s struggles with sleep, the negative reactions to medications she was prescribed, anxiety about returning to work and leaving her children as well as intrusive thoughts that include wanting to hurt herself.
But he noted that at a psychiatric hospital she stayed about two weeks before she killed her children that she never reported having hallucinations or suicidal thoughts. Her main concern was insomnia.
Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty to murder charges in the deaths of Callan, Dawson and Cora Clancy, who ranged from 8 months to 5 years old.
The two sides have presented experts with starkly contradicting testimony on whether Clancy was suffering from postpartum psychosis.
After the defense rested Friday, prosecutors began calling rebuttal witnesses, starting with Mack. He agreed that Clancy suffered from a major depressive episode but said he found no evidence of mania or hypomania to support a bipolar diagnosis — or of psychosis.

Sudanese army chief vows to defeat RSF, dismisses no-fly zone rumors

Adel Abdelrheem, Mohammad Sio
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Sudanese army chief and Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan on Monday vowed to defeat the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and restore security nationwide, urging Sudanese citizens to ignore reports about possible sanctions against Sudan.
Al-Burhan made the remarks at a graduation ceremony for military cadets at Khartoum’s Police Sciences and Law College, according to a statement released by the Sovereignty Council.
“We assure the Sudanese people that the armed forces, backed by other regular forces, are moving toward restoring security and stability across the country,” al-Burhan said.
Referring to the RSF, he said the paramilitary group would “be defeated, and citizens will return to their areas and villages to resume their normal lives.”
Sudan has been engulfed by a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023 -- a conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced 13 million others, according to UN and international estimates.
“Ongoing talk of possible sanctions against Sudan will not affect us or weaken our resolve,” al-Burhan said, adding that the country’s destiny was “in God’s hands.”
He also called on the Sudanese people to ignore claims by “malicious actors” regarding the imposition of a no-fly zone over Sudan, vowing to continue what he called the “battle for dignity” until “every inch of Sudanese land” is liberated.
In recent days, reports have emerged about a possible US proposal to impose a no-fly zone over parts of Sudan controlled by the army and the RSF.   
Juba Peace Agreement
On the implementation of the Juba Peace Agreement, al-Burhan said the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), led by Sovereignty Council Deputy Chairman Malik Agar, had joined the army with all its forces.
Al-Burhan went on to urge other armed factions to follow suit.
Khartoum signed a peace agreement with armed groups belonging to the Sudan Revolutionary Front in 2020.
The agreement did not include the Sudan Liberation Army led by Abdel Wahid Mohamed Nur or the SPLM-N led by Abdelaziz al-Hilu.

How close are Russia and the UK to war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:50:21 UTC
03:50:21 KST

How close are Russia and the UK to war?
Russia just pulled its ambassador to the UK, as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham doubles down on open involvement in the Ukraine conflict. The risk of open war has never been higher, but Burnham is writing checks that he can’t cash.
Relations between Russia and the UK are at an “unprecedentedly low level,” Moscow’s embassy in London said in a statement on Sunday, after it emerged that ambassador Andrey Kelin had left his post in late July and would not be immediately replaced. In a follow-up statement to the Sunday Times, an embassy spokesperson said that Kelin had made “considerable efforts to preserve contacts and channels of communication” between the UK and Russia, but the UK had clearly chosen a “path of confrontation.”
☝️ Russia-UK relations across all areas have deteriorated to an unprecedentedly low level entirely on London's initiative.https://t.co/ddib4uE1B4pic.twitter.com/BrdJAyk4bO
— Russian Embassy, UK (@RussianEmbassy) August 23, 2026
“He left Britain in the hope that a more constructive and respectful dialogue could eventually be restored, should the UK reconsider its policies towards our country,” the spokesman added.
How did Russia/UK relations get this bad?
Well, firstly, Keir Starmer, Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson, Theresa May, and of course David Cameron and their anglophonic media bullhorns.
Moscow has viewed the UK as one of Ukraine’s most bellicose foreign backers since the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022. Former Prime Minister Boris Johnson intervened to scupper a peace deal between Moscow and Kiev that April; Britain supplied Ukraine with ‘Storm Shadow’ cruise missiles for long-range strikes on Russia a year later; and in the latest revelation by the British press, Ukraine utilized a plethora of British-made drones in its campaign of long-range attacks on Russian civilian targets this year.
On August 17, the Russian embassy in London warned Britain that “the deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kiev’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov added that Moscow has “every right to regard the proudly proclaimed direct involvement of British missile forces in strikes against Russia as participation in the war, with all the consequences that entails.”
Neither statement seems to have deterred Burnham. Later that day, the British PM proclaimed that the UK would continue “to support Ukraine 100%.” Six days later, his office announced that it would provide Ukraine with classified information enabling it to produce Storm Shadow cruise missiles on Ukrainian soil. Burnham followed this up with a visit to Kiev on Monday, where he compared the conflict to Britain’s struggle against Nazi Germany in World War II, and promised to supply Ukraine with anti-air missiles to repel Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
Is pulling the ambassador a sign of war?
The withdrawal of Kelin is an unprecedented move. Diplomatic relations between Moscow and London have been strained on multiple occasions during the post-Soviet period, Russia’s response has typically been restrained. When FSB agents caught British spies hiding a listening device outside the Russian embassy in 2006, the Kremlin named and condemned the agents responsible. When the UK expelled four Russian diplomats after Moscow refused to extradite a suspect in the alleged poisoning of double agent Alexander Litvinenko in 2007, Russia responded in kind.
Similarly, when the UK expelled 23 diplomats in 2018 over the alleged poisoning of undercover MI6 agent Sergei Skripal, Moscow’s response was the tit-for-tat expulsion of 23 Brits staff and the closure of a British consulate-general in St. Petersburg.
At no point during these incidents did Russia withdraw – or threaten to withdraw – its ambassador. However, with relations already in the gutter since 2022, Moscow’s lack of urgency in replacing Kelin most likely does not herald military action against the UK. Instead, it is an acknowledgement of just how badly relations have deteriorated.
What will Russia do to neutralize the UK’s Ukraine missile threat?
Russia’s kinetic response to Burnham’s missile data sharing plan is straightforward. In a statement to reporters on August 24, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that “our armed forces are carrying out the relevant work and obtaining the necessary data in order to identify the production sites for such missiles and other military equipment, and are taking measures to destroy these locations.”
Destroying missile production sites in Ukraine is a far easier task for Russia now than at any point since 2022. Ukraine has no ammunition for its Patriot air defense batteries left, nor does Kiev have any money to buy more. In a post on X on Sunday, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky admitted that his military used all of its 2026 budget in the first six months of the year buying and building drones to attack civilian infrastructure in Russia.
As a result, Russia has been dismantling weapons plants, ports and ships used to import arms, and energy targets across Ukraine with impunity since July.
How far can Britain escalate against Russia?
Burnham has little more to offer. The US is unwilling to share its dwindling stocks of Patriot missiles with Ukraine, even if the UK offers to buy. Three out of five weapons packages donated by the UK to Ukraine this year included other models of defense missiles – a total of more than 2,500 missiles – but these have apparently been used up by Kiev’s forces.
Britain’s ability to escalate beyond data-sharing and weapons packages is constrained by two key factors. Firstly, open UK intervention in Ukraine could trigger a cataclysmic, and likely nuclear, conflict between Russia and NATO. Secondly, Britain’s armed forces have been hollowed out by decades of underfunding: there are fewer active-duty troops in the British military than at any point since the end of the Napoleonic Wars; Britain reportedly has enough ammunition for less than a day of full-scale combat; and no means of defense against Russian ballistic missiles.
Given the potential consequences, some figures within the British defense establishment have called for restraint. Former Chief of the Defense Staff Tony Radakin – who once urged Britain to prepare to fight Russia in space – and his successor, Richard Knighton, have both reportedly sought contact with Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov in order to limit the threat of naval escalation. Another former British defense chief, Field Marshal Lord David Richards, has called for peace talks with Russia since 2022, arguing last year that Ukraine “cannot win” the conflict with anything short of full-scale NATO intervention.
Even former defense attache John Foreman – who has encouraged Ukraine to strike Russia with British-made missiles – told The Times on August 15 that Britain should reopen “strategic dialog” with Russia, calling London’s suspension of military-to-military communications in 2024 “daft.”
'Good to speak to @edvaizey today about the need to hold our noses and re-establish mil to mil ties.
We can continue to support Ukraine. But at the same time, we can talk to the Russians'. Cutting military communication with Russia was a 'daft decision'.
With Russian forces…
These calls have also come from the UK’s typically hawkish circuit of ‘Russia experts’. Among this group is Mark Galeotti, an academic with rumored links to British intelligence. In an interview with former British diplomat Ian Proud in mid-August, Galeotti conceded that “behind closed doors,” many British diplomatic and security officials now believe that “we’ve reached the stage where we need to be pushing both sides to some kind of resolution.”
“After years of spouting these empty mantras of ‘as much as it takes, for as long as it takes’, etc etc, who’s going to turn around and say ‘actually, come to think of it, this is not in our interests’,” he told Proud.
Will Burnham step back?
Burnham, Galeotti argued, is unlikely to spend precious political capital on restarting diplomacy with Russia, as to do so would open him up to attacks from rival parties and hawks within his own Labour Party.
After his speech in Kiev on Monday, Burnham chaired a meeting of the ‘coalition of the willing’ – a 34-nation group put together to pool military aid for Ukraine. In his opening remarks, Burnham called on the UK’s allies to “dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks” to keep the Ukrainian military fighting.
However, should the UK continue supplying long-range missiles and drones to Ukraine, and should these munitions be used to kill Russian civilians, Russia is running out of diplomatic means of deterring London.
Britain has scoffed at every polite warning from Moscow to date, but with Kelin’s office vacant, there are fewer civilized options available to Russia. The “consequences” threatened by Lavrov could be far more catastrophic than a formal demarche.

Ex-Pussy Riot member says FSB coerced her into three years of informing on Russian artists and activists, then told her to help kidnap and kill Pyotr Verzilov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:49:29 UTC

Ex-Pussy Riot member says FSB coerced her into three years of informing on Russian artists and activists, then told her to help kidnap and kill Pyotr Verzilov
Former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores (real name Margarita Konovalova) said she began cooperating with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) in 2023, helping the agency gather information on contemporary artists and political activists, including members of Pussy Riot.
Flores described her work for the FSB in an interview with defense attorney Dmitry Zakhvatov, who helped her leave Russia. The outlet Port published both a video and a written summary of the interview.
She met an FSB officer named Ivan — the man who would become her handler — after agents searched her apartment on February 17, 2023. At the time, she was reported to have gone missing after the search. While others searched for her, she was at home with two FSB officers, who coerced her into cooperating. They threatened her with criminal prosecution, said they would kill her relatives, and warned that she herself would “disappear without a trace” if she refused to work for them.
The FSB gave Flores the code name “Harley,” began training her “as an agent,” confiscated all of her documents except her internal Russian passport, and issued her a “work” phone.
Her main job for the FSB was to flag artworks that could give the agency grounds to begin targeting their creators and to compile a “report” on someone the agency planned to prosecute. In that report, she was to lay out the person’s background, relatives and close contacts, habits, and vulnerabilities.
Flores said she took part in the FSB’s targeting of street artist Filipp Kozlov, who works under the name Philippenzo; performance artist Pavel Krisevich; and fellow Pussy Riot member Maria Alyokhina. She said the FSB also tried to enlist her in the kidnapping and murder of Pyotr Verzilov, Mediazona’s former publisher and a member of the art groups Voina and Pussy Riot.
After being handed the Verzilov assignment, Flores contacted Zakhvatov. With his help, she persuaded her handlers to “postpone” the job, then fled the country. Neither she nor Zakhvatov would say how she got out. Flores got in touch with him in the summer of 2025, Zakhvatov said, and she was brought out of Russia about 10 days ago.
Flores said she decided to go public about her work for the FSB to help others in similar situations. On Instagram, she thanked Zakhvatov and former Yukos executive Leonid Nevzlin for their help, saying the two men had “saved her ass and her soul.”
Philippenzo responded to Flores’ statements by sending Meduza an image of a 2017 painting of his that was seized during searches of his studio in 2023.

Ukraine got independence as a gift in 1991. Now we pay in blood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:49:18 UTC
03:49:18 KST

In 1991, Ukraine did not shed a drop of blood. It was a transition of power. We raised a flag, we declared ourselves independent, and we received our independence as a gift.
Now we are shedding rivers of blood for real independence.
That is the difference between this Independence Day and the ones before it, and I do not think we have absorbed it yet.
Colonial theory has a name for what happened to us thirty-five years ago. It is called flag independence. You raise the flag, you declare the state, and for a while you believe that was it—that this was the end, and now we simply continue as an independent nation.
In theory it was believed to be like that. In practice, every decolonized nation eventually discovered the same thing: it is not the end. It is the beginning.
The nations that gathered at Bandung in Indonesia in 1955 worked this out before us. They had their flags. They also had the former metropolis still holding the strings—to their economies, their cultures, their political classes. They named it: neocolonialism.
And they understood that real independence would take something longer and harder than a declaration. Not only liberation with arms, but liberation of the mind from the colonial legacy. Not erasing the colonial memory—reworking it, synthesizing it into something new.
So here is the shape of it. Before 1991, Ukrainians waged a struggle for independence without statehood. After 1991, we have been waging a struggle for independence within statehood. The struggle did not end. It changed its conditions.
What was gathered into the Act of Independence
The declaration was a beginning, but it was also a result—of generations.
It begins in the nineteenth century, with people like Taras Shevchenko, who essentially invented a Ukrainian identity. It was a construction. It was not, as Putin claims, the invention of Vladimir Lenin. It was the invention of Ukrainian intellectuals, writers, and religious leaders, who constructed this nation on the basis of what came before—the Cossack Republic, Kyivan Rus, the long stretch from the Middle Ages through early modernity.
Then the dissidents of the Soviet period. Then the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which fought on two fronts against three colonizers: the Germans, the Poles, and the Soviets. Their struggle was clearly anti-colonial. Brutal, but anti-colonial. I do not justify everything they did. I am applying postcolonial theory in order to make sense of what they did, or tried to do. They were defeated. Their ideas resurfaced in 1991 and were gathered into the Act of Independence.
And that Act, while it closed a long period of Ukrainian struggle without a state, opened a new one.
Today, more independence than colonialism
Before 2013, I would say, there was more neocolonialism than independence.
This is a description, not a figure of speech. The former metropolis re-established the strings. Russian capital came into the economy under the presidencies of Leonid Kuchma and Viktor Yanukovych, and Russian corruption came with it.
Proxy parties were planted—the Party of Regions and its various clones. Russian pop music was everywhere, which sounds like a small thing and is not: in postcolonial studies, literature and popular culture are considered among the most effective vehicles of neocolonial control.
Today it is the other way around. Neocolonialism has not evaporated, but the proportion has changed. There is now more independence than neocolonialism—and that itself is what thirty-five years of struggle have achieved.
And corruption was a neocolonial instrument. This is the part Ukrainians resist, so let me put it plainly: our fight against corruption is effectively an anti-colonial fight. In Ukraine people sometimes present this as a dilemma—either we fight corruption or we fight the Russians, we cannot do both. From the perspective of postcolonial studies the dilemma does not exist. Both are anti-colonial efforts. They go hand in hand.
Empires have always travelled with religion on their shoulders, and religion has always helped establish imperial rule in the colonies. In the Ukrainian case it was first the Greek Catholic Church, established in 1596 an instrument of Polish colonization, although this is not the case anymore. But that is how it began.
And presently Russia’s instrument of recolonization is the Moscow Patriarchate, still present in Ukraine as the Ukrainian Orthodox Church under the Moscow Patriarchate (UOC MP).
Anatomy of treason: how the Ukrainian Orthodox Church sold its soul to the “Russian world”
Here I have to say something uncomfortable for many Ukrainians.
Nations that decolonize very often produce new subalterns. In post-colonial language, these are parts of the population that are subdued, oppressed by the dominant power. But we may be producing such subalterns as an effect of pushing back against Russian colonization: groups of Ukrainians belonging to the UOC MP being marginalized, subalternized, by our own struggle. It is a very difficult dilemma how to deal with this subalternization, and I do not have a resolution for it.
Two revolutions against the ratio
Both of Ukraine’s major “Maidan” protests were anti-neocolonial revolutions.
In the Orange Revolution of 2004 and again during the Euromaidan Revolution in 2013, Ukrainians protested because they had decided there was not enough independence—that what we had was more neocolonial than independent, more fake than real, and that the proportion had to be corrected. That is what a Maidan is. A public consensus that the ratio is wrong.
In February 2022, independence very nearly ended. People gave our statehood three days—and not only Russians. That was the opinion of most observers. It did not end. We survived it. But our statehood is still not secured, and it is being secured every day, including today.
What Ukraine contributed to the empire, and how
There is an argument against everything I have said so far, and Ukrainians make it as often as anyone. They object: look, we have contributed to the Russian Empire and to the Soviet one. We have basically built them.
Which is true.
Ukraine helped build the Russian empire. Now it stands in the way of its resurrection – Serhii Plokhii
But Ukrainians were never permitted to contribute as independent agents. They were allowed to contribute exactly as long as they lost their identity—as long as they denounced their own agency. They were contributors without their will and without their identity.
Corsica is my example. It had its own culture, its own identity, its own language, still spoken in pockets. Go into a good Corsican restaurant in Corsica and they may speak Corsican to you; I have had this experience. But it is not a language widely spoken anymore. It has been completely subsumed by French, and France holds Corsica tightly today. And what is France? To a great extent, it is the creature of a great Corsican named Napoleon Bonaparte, who built the French Empire. Nobody concludes from this that Corsica was not a colony.
It is remarkable to me that Putin still does this. He puts people with Ukrainian backgrounds into key positions—in the military, in propaganda, in negotiations.
- Vladimir Medinsky, one of his chief propagandists and now his negotiator, was born in Smila, in Cherkasy Oblast, my own small motherland.
- Valentina Matviyenko, third in the official hierarchy, comes from Shepetivka in Khmelnytskyi Oblast.
- Kirill Dmitriev, who negotiates with the Americans, was born in Kyiv to a family of Ukrainian biologists.
It was Medinsky, incidentally, who announced in a 2012 interview that the Russian people has one extra chromosome—his explanation for how Russia survived the catastrophes of the twentieth century when other nations, the Scythians and Sarmatians among them, broke and vanished. Russians mocked him for it, since an extra chromosome is the marker of Down syndrome.
As a claim, though, it is a race claim. Made by a man born in Cherkasy Oblast, about a people he was not born into.
They contribute to the Russian neo-empire. They contribute to it not as Ukrainians but as those who denounced Ukrainian identity. This is how empire functions. It absorbs the representatives of subaltern nations who willingly denounce their own will. It was so under the Romanovs. It was so in the Soviet empire. It is so in Putin's quasi-empire now.
Ukrainians were, and still are, a subaltern nation.
Papua, and Scotland
There are worse outcomes than ours and there are better ones.
The Papuans of West Papua tried. They fought for independence, failed, and many of them were killed. They are still oppressed. That is the bad end of the range, and it is not hypothetical.
The better scenario would be the Scots. They had statehood, and it was strong—kings and queens, pride, history, narratives, everything a full and self-sufficient nation possesses. Then they lost it. They are not being killed. They do not suffer the way the Papuans suffer. And yet many of them remain deeply dissatisfied with what they are. We support the United Kingdom, of course, but we are also mindful of the peoples who constitute it—Scots, Irish, Welsh. They have their pride, their nation, their language, their history, their self-consciousness, their identity.
They cannot fully live any of it without independence.
That would be a much better scenario for us than the Papuan one. From where we are now, I still do not think it would be enough.
Colonies taken by neighbors
Timor-Leste has stayed with me. One of the newest countries in the world, independent since 2002, and before that a genocide. Up to a third of its population died. Its capital, Dili, was destroyed in 1999.
Our own Baturyn, the capital of the Cossack Hetmanate, was destroyed by Peter I's army in 1708 in the same way.
And Timor is not an overseas colony. That is the other thing. There is the colonization conducted across an ocean—the Dutch in the Malay Archipelago, to which Timor belongs—and there is the colonization conducted by a neighbor. Indonesia, having been a Dutch colony itself, became independent, developed a colonial attitude within thirty years, and invaded Timor.
Ukraine was taken by neighbors too. First Poland, then the Russian Empire. Both committed atrocities here. We always resisted, and always with some violence—there has never been an anti-colonial struggle that was not violent, and ours is not an exception. I wish it were an exception. It was not.
The first colonization, and the first decolonization
The Polish colonization is the one Ukrainians forget, and it matters for a reason that has nothing to do with Poland.
It ended. And the decolonization from it was successful: we regained our ground, re-established Ukrainian identity on our territory, our own way of living. And there was a process of reconciliation that worked, at least to some extent. That is the first decolonization Ukrainians ever accomplished, and it is the paradigm I hold onto when I think about what happens with Russia.
Which does not mean it is finished. Some of the reactions coming from the Polish side now are, to me, surprising and incomprehensible, and I can explain them only through this lens: post-colonial phantom pain. They lost a limb and they still feel it. Russia feels the same phantom pain about what it calls the Russian World, and reacts far more violently, because Russia is historically far more violent. But the pain is the same kind of pain.
One white nation killing another
Much of the world does not accept that any of this is decolonization. In the Global South the response is: one white nation is killing another white nation, why should we care.
They should care, because our struggle is the same as theirs was. If ours is meaningless, then theirs was meaningless too.
They are working with a black and white colonial paradigm—sometimes literally—which skims over the surface. There is a name for what we are: a South within the North. Inside the Global North pockets of land and people exist whose experience and self-perception are closer to the peoples of the Global South than to their neighbors. Ukraine is one of those pockets. Our vision of ourselves may be nearer to the Global South than to Europe.
Race is the real difference, and I will not pretend otherwise. Though even there the resemblance is closer than people assume. When we were a Polish colony, the Poles developed the idea that we were an inferior people—chłopy—while they were Sarmatians, a superior nation. Not race as skin color. Race as ethnic origin, which does the same work.
By my own study, something like 90% of the criteria that apply to other colonies apply to Ukraine. Perhaps 10% do not.
But before the world can see this, we Ukrainians have to see it.
Why the blood
Fanon believed that violence is embedded in colonialism—that it is intrinsic, that you cannot be a colonial power without being violent, without being prepared to kill the subalterns. He also believed that anticolonial struggle is inevitably violent. Sartre, who wrote the preface to him, believed it too. Maybe that is right, and it would be a good and easy explanation.
But our struggle is particularly bloody for a particular reason, and it is Russian. Russia has adopted most of its ideas from the West, and has almost always put them into practice through violence exceeding anything done in the place the idea came from. Marxist ideas about the counter-revolutionary nature of the peasantry produced the Holodomor; American culture wars are producing this one.
Our resistance is violent because their aggression is. It is a reaction, and it does not exceed the action. If anything it is disproportionate in the other direction. They kill our civilians in daylight and destroy hospitals and residential buildings. We destroy their oil plants and the warehouses of their online marketplaces.
From the standpoint of genocide studies, what is being done to us is a classical genocide. Not a rhetorical trope—a scientifically provable case. What is unprecedented is not the death toll but the intensity: the quantity of weaponry and ammunition involved in this anti-colonial war has no precedent among anti-colonial wars.
Agency
This is what Ukraine has to contribute to postcolonial theory, and I think it is the important thing.
The victims are not powerless and they are not will-less. They have their own volition. They have their own agency. And the purpose of an anti-colonial struggle is to regain agency—not merely independence, not merely economic freedom, not merely the cutting of ties with international capital or with the old and new empires. Agency.
Our struggle is a struggle for and through our agency. And it is a path that other peoples still living with the residues of colonialism could follow.
The neocolonialism that is not Russian
The Russian form is the most obvious available to us. It is not the only one.
The newest arrived with the Trump administration, which tried to exchange support for our resources—rare earth elements and so forth—essentially requiring us to give them up in return for help. This is a classical neocolonial attitude. It is what happens when a neocolonial power is being established.
I want to be careful here, because this is the policy of the White House and not of Americans. Most Americans who come to Ukraine come as volunteers, prepared to sacrifice their lives, because they understand that global democracy depends on what happens here. The neocolonial attitude belongs to a minority. Unfortunately, that minority currently holds power.
It is a new situation for us, but it is not unique for the world. Still, we can survive it if we understand what it is.
Russia is the last European colonial empire, but the West looks away. Expert explains why
Whether it is worth it
It is not for us to answer that.
Our generation has decided that it is worth it. But we should remember that we have also decided for the next generation. The Ukrainian Sich Riflemen, a volunteer legion of students and intelligentsia raised in Lviv in 1914, decided in their time that it was worth sacrificing themselves for Ukrainian independence, and we now judge that they were right. The UPA, fighting into the 1950s, decided the same. They were defeated.
We do not know how the next generation will judge us. Because there will be millions of Ukrainians who will not have been born as a result of this war. They will not decide whether we were right or wrong. They will not exist.
Those who do exist will make the judgment.

US revokes Syria’s designation as State Sponsor of Terrorism — Treasury Department
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:49:06 UTC
03:49:06 KST

WASHINGTON, August 24. /TASS/. The United States has officially revoked Syria’s designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism and the designation of Syria’s Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS, outlawed in Russia) as a terrorist organization, the press service of the US Department of the Treasury said.
"In line with President [Donald] Trump’s promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria, the U.S. Department of State today rescinded Syria’s designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism, and revoked the designation of al-Nusrah Front, also known as Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT) organization. Concurrently, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) removed HTS from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List ("SDN List")," it said.
Concurrently, it imposed sanctions against two former HTS affiliates who continue to support al-Qaeda (outlawed in Russia).
The U.S. Department of the Treasury may take action against legal entities, individuals, and countries that engage in trade with countries on the list of state sponsors of terrorism. Currently, the list includes Iran, North Korea, and Cuba.

US unveils ‘economic onslaught’ against Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
