02:01:58 KST

A protest speaker said that Zionists rape, kill, and eat children, and he invoked other conspiracy theories at a demonstration in the Jewish neighborhood of Bathurst Street and Sheppard Avenue West in Toronto yesterday.
Video footage of the speech was shared on social media by the X/Twitter account Leviathan, identifying it as taking place at a pro-Palestine protest that took place yesterday.
Leviathan is an X account dedicated, in its words, to naming “Jihadists, Antisemites, Anarchists & other threats. Using OSINT [open-source intelligence] to notify for Public Interest” in Canada.
According to the account, the speaker is a Toronto-based university instructor and faculty lecturer named Abbas Hamze.
Speaker invokes antisemitic conspiracy theories at Toronto protest
The video captures a speaker telling an audience, “The British colonizers have planted this cancerous, this cancerous, false Zionist state of Israel. It’s Falasteen [Palestine].”
He asserted, “These Zionists have never had a country of their own because of their mischief; they are the most kicked-out people in the world for making black magic and horrible things.”
He further said, “We can see the corruption crystal clear in the Epstein Island where they have seduced leaders from all around the world, including Trump. They have raped and killed and eaten children at the same time. They have done the unimaginable to blackmail them and control them.”
In a separate post on X from May, Leviathan wrote, “Hamze is a Master Sessional & Master of Data Analytics Instructor with University of Niagara Falls, a Faculty Lecturer at Georgian College, and a College Lecturer for Conestoga College.”
It added, “Abbas Hamze also calls for the kidnapping of Israeli hostages, stating that ‘Hamas has the right to take hostages on October 7th 2023,’ while also claiming ‘Hezbollah has the right to assist Hamas on October 8th,’” Leviathan wrote, citing alleged social media posts by Hamze.
Leviathan said that the Toronto Police Service had provided Hamze with “an armed escort” as he “protests at Jewish neighborhoods, schools, and synagogues” and that he “came to Canada from France in August of 2022 & is not believed to be a Canadian citizen.”
Referring to accompanying screenshots alleged to be from Hamze’s social media posts, Leviathan added, “Abbas Hamze has also been pictured holding up flags of the Islamic Republic of Iran in this Jewish neighborhood while also writing, ‘We will continue the path of Imam Khamenei, no matter how many sacrifices are made, and his pure blood will bear the inevitable victory.’”
B’nai Brith calls on Toronto Police to investigate
Richard Robertson, B’nai Brith Canada’s director of Research and Advocacy, said in a statement to The Jerusalem Post, “The ongoing anti-Israel protests at Bathurst and Sheppard continue to be a source of hate and incitement.
“Incidents such as those which occurred this weekend are the result of the permissive environment that has been created at the intersection since October 7, 2023. Antisemitism is becoming normalized on Toronto’s streets.”
He added, “When classical antisemitic tropes, such as that Jews use ‘black magic’ and eat children, are broadcast in public using a megaphone, there is no ambiguity. It is the wilful promotion and public incitement of hate.
“Toronto Police must investigate the incident as such and hold those responsible accountable. They must also reexamine their approach to protests at Bathurst and Sheppard; there must be a zero tolerance for turning our streets into platforms from which to incite and promote hatred.”
Recurring Toronto protests draw scrutiny amid antisemitism concerns
The demonstration took place amid heightened tensions surrounding recurring protests at the Bathurst Street and Sheppard Avenue West intersection.
These regular rallies in the heavily Jewish residential neighborhood have drawn intense community concern and scrutiny, leading to multiple police interventions and the recent arrest of activists, including two individuals detained by the Toronto Police Service on charges of the willful promotion of hatred and public incitement of hatred.
Ongoing hate propaganda investigations stem from demonstrations earlier in the year when suspects allegedly retrieved antisemitic signs from a storage locker before marching toward counter-protesters while shouting derogatory slurs.
In recent months, there has been a broader national surge in antisemitic attacks targeting Jewish and Israeli institutions across Canada.
According to reports and tracking data released by advocacy groups such as B’nai Brith Canada and the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (CIJA), violent offenses have risen sharply, marked by high-profile episodes such as targeted shootings and vandalism at Jewish-owned commercial establishments like branches of Toronto’s Kiva’s Bagel Bar, gunfire incidents directed at Jewish schools, and a suspected arson attack targeting the kosher establishment Nöam restaurant in Montreal.

Pakistan army chief meets with Iran president in Tehran
Pakistan's powerful army chief Asim Munir met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran on Monday, state television reported, as Islamabad tries to mediate a resolution to the Middle East war.
The meeting took place after US President Donald Trump spoke last week with Munir, a US source familiar with the matter told AFP earlier on Monday.
Pakistan has played a key role in efforts to halt the conflict between Iran and the United States, brokering a memorandum of understanding in June, but peace negotiations currently appear stalled.
Munir also met in Tehran with Iran's parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, as well as Mohsen Rezaei, head of the country's highest national security body, according to Iranian state television.
Iran's foreign ministry had said on Sunday that Munir's visit would be part of "Pakistan's ongoing efforts to help consolidate peace and security in the region".
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, expanding Washington's secondary sanctions threats and warning of dire consequences for countries that do not join the campaign.
Israel's Netanyahu says Iran tried to kill one of his sons
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Monday that Iran had tried to kill one of his sons, but gave no details about when the alleged plot took place, which son was targeted or how close it came to being carried out.
Netanyahu's allegation underscores the heightened tensions since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began in February, during which Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other senior Iranian leaders were killed.
Netanyahu, whose coalition is trailing in opinion polls two months before an October 27 general election, made the claim in a telephone interview with Israel's Channel 14. He was responding to reports that one of Israel's security agencies had refused to provide protection for a political rival ahead of the nationwide vote.
"As for my sons. Here, I think there is something quite unbelievable, yes. Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to kill, to murder one of my sons," Netanyahu told the conservative channel known for its favourable coverage of the government.
'Major financial institution' faces US sanction over Iran
In his ongoing press conference, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a major financial institution would be sanctioned over Iran by the end of the week.
"You will see a major financial institution being sanctioned by the end of this week over Iran," Bessent said
US threatens dollar ban over Iran money laundering
More from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's press conference announcing a raft of economic measures against Iran.
Bessent is now saying that Washington would end access to the US dollar system for those laundering Iranian money, as he sought to ramp up pressure targeting Tehran months into war.
"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking."
Bessent warns world against economic engagement with Iran
Bessent says new US sanctions aim to block all potential sources of revenue for Iran, tells nations to cut economic ties.
“Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has told a news conference.
In his latest Truth Social post, US President Donald Trump again claimed the US was "winning" against Iran, while accusing Democrats of publishing "fake polls" aimed at "demoralizing Republicans".
"The Radical Left Democrats are going CRAZY with Fake Polls. They’re putting them out at levels never seen before. They’re called, ‘Demoralization Operations,’ where they try to demoralize Republicans so that they don’t go out and vote — But the actual Polls are tremendous, and the Spirit in our Country has never been higher. We’re winning against EVERYONE, including Iran, whose Country is in Economic and Military Death Spiral," Trump wrote.
Iran warns of strikes on US energy chokepoints if attacked
Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), has warned of "heavy attacks on US energy chokepoints and vital interests" if Iranian infrastructure is targeted, according to state broadcaster IRIB.
"Any attack on Iran's infrastructure will bring heavy strikes on US energy chokepoints and vital interests," Mohebbi was quoted as saying.
He said US objectives, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz, had been thwarted, while Iran continued to produce weapons.
"Contrary to the enemy's perception that Iran's military had limited reserves, the production of our smart and guided missiles continues," he said

====================================================================================================

Israel’s Syria strike may have jolted diplomacy back to life - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:01:12 UTC
02:01:12 KST

Israel’s attack on the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northern Syria last week did not end Israeli-Syrian diplomacy, as some initially feared. In fact, it may have accelerated it.
That does not mean the attack was without risk. Striking an airbase shortly after a Turkish delegation reportedly visited the site could have triggered a direct clash with Turkey on Syrian soil.
But the strike also concentrated minds. On Sunday, five days later, Mossad head Roman Gofman and Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani met in Jordan for US-mediated talks aimed at lowering tensions and preventing another such incident.
The meeting mattered not only because of who attended, but because it marked the resumption of a diplomatic process suspended since the outbreak of the Iran war at the end of February.
According to reports, the talks dealt with reviving Israeli-Syrian security negotiations and preventing mounting Israel-Turkey tensions from spilling over into Syrian territory.
The sides also reportedly discussed establishing a special operations or coordination room in Jordan under US supervision. Its purpose would be to provide a channel through which Israel, Syria, and possibly Turkey could communicate and prevent misunderstandings from escalating into military confrontations.
That Turkey is now a central part of the Israeli-Syrian agenda is itself one consequence of the Abu al-Duhur attack and something Jerusalem welcomes.
IDF strike placed Turkish involvement in Syria at international forefront
Before the strike, Ankara’s growing military involvement in Syria was largely treated as an issue between Turkey and Syria. Israel’s action placed it at the forefront of the international agenda. It served notice that Jerusalem views a Turkish military presence in Syria not as an internal Syrian issue but as a potential threat to Israeli security.
Regardless of whether one accepts Israel’s intelligence assessment that Turkey was going to move weapons systems and personnel into the airbase or Syria’s insistence that no Turkish base was planned, the danger is now impossible to ignore. Turkey is heavily invested in rebuilding and training Syria’s army, while Israel has now made clear that there are limits to a Turkish military presence it is willing to tolerate.
The choice of Jordan as the venue for the talks – and as the possible home of a deconfliction mechanism – is also telling.
Earlier rounds of Israeli-Syrian talks were held in places such as Paris and Baku, far from the region. Jordan, by contrast, borders both Israel and Syria and has a vested interest in preventing a possible war on its doorstep.
Jordan also offers an instructive reminder.
Diplomatic relations between Jerusalem and Amman are cold and frequently confrontational, despite the peace treaty between the two countries. The two governments disagree sharply and publicly over the Palestinians, Gaza, and Jerusalem. Yet beneath that political hostility, they maintain extensive security coordination because it benefits them both.
Israel and Syria are obviously in a different position: They remain formally at war and have no diplomatic relations. But Jordan demonstrates that political warmth is not a prerequisite for practical security coordination. That may be what Washington is seeking for Israel and Syria at this stage – not warm relations, certainly not a peace treaty, but a mechanism to prevent their disputes from repeatedly threatening to erupt into war.
Which is essentially what is currently on the table.
Damascus wants Israel to withdraw to the positions it held before the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024 and to restore the 1974 disengagement framework. It also rejects Israeli demands placing limits on the weapons systems it can introduce and the degree of military assistance it can accept from Turkey.
Israel, meanwhile, reportedly wants southern Syria to remain demilitarized, restrictions placed on Syrian weaponry, guarantees for the Druze, and an end to Turkish military activity in Syria.
Those positions remain far apart. Syria sees Israeli demands as an infringement on its sovereignty, while Israel views Damascus’s insistence on rebuilding its military with Turkish assistance as providing an open door for a very hostile regional power to establish itself on Israel’s northern border.
The talks in Jordan will not quickly bridge that gap. But they may help establish rules for managing it.
Diplomatic fallout from strike includes gains despite criticism
Israel may therefore have gained something diplomatically from the Abu al-Duhur strike, despite the fierce criticism it generated. Turkey’s military presence in Syria is now the subject of a US-mediated process, not merely an Israeli concern that Ankara and Damascus can easily dismiss.
But Israel must be careful not to overplay its hand.
A demand that there be no Turkish military activity anywhere in Syria is much more than either Damascus or Ankara is likely to accept. Syria regards Turkey as a critical partner in rebuilding the state after more than a decade of civil war. Ankara, meanwhile, has invested too much political, military, and economic capital in the new Syrian order to allow Israel an effective veto over its role there.
The more realistic objective would be clearly defined restrictions. This could mean no Turkish bases or state-of-the-art air defense systems in areas Israel considers vital to its national security; advance notice of significant deployments; and a dependable communications mechanism to prevent either side from misreading the other’s intentions.
The Abu al-Duhur strike did not resolve the problem. It did, however, make clear what is at stake and force the danger of an Israeli-Turkish collision directly onto the diplomatic agenda.
The bombs dropped on Abu al-Duhur’s runways, as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said afterward, delivered a message that was not heeded via the established diplomatic channels. The Jordan talks will determine whether that message – so dramatically delivered – can now actually produce a workable arrangement.

Bessent warns countries defying US sanctions will 'share in isolation' of Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:00:41 UTC
02:00:41 KST

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that any country that continues to enable Iran will become part of US efforts to "isolate" Tehran from the global economy, adding that US President Donald Trump is already calling on world leaders to halt trade with Iran.
Bessent unveiled new sanctions on Iran on Monday — targeting Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping — escalating the Trump administration’s pressure on Tehran to negotiate a deal to end the conflict and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
"Iran's enablers purchase, transport its petroleum. They facilitate the flow of its finances through exchange houses and free trade zones. They welcome Iran's flights and maintain registries on its behalf. They turn a blind eye to seaborne fuel transfers and overland transits. They condone illicit use of their banks, all the while concealing the extent of their complicity," Bessent told media in Washington DC, without naming the countries.
He said every country has a defined timeline to shut down activities the US has identified, warning, "If they do not take action, we will do so unilaterally through Treasury authorities."
He said President Trump is making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with Iran.
"We are already seeing results over the weekend," he added.
View on China
Bessent said that countries and entities that stand with the US "will reap the rewards of our partnership", but warned "those who tether themselves to the Iranian regime should expect to share in the isolation of a withering regime."
He stated that delegations from the US Treasury, State Department, and military are engaging international counterparts to urge decisive action.
Bessent said that Washington would end access to the US dollar system for those laundering Iranian money, as he sought to ramp up pressure targeting Tehran months into war.
"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking."
Analysts say the impact of Bessent's announcement hinges on whether Iran's key trading partners, such as China, view US warnings as credible.
Asked if Chinese banks dealing with Iran could be targeted, Bessent said "no one is above the reach of US sanctions."
"An economic engagement of any kind with this murderous regime will expose those responsible to the full reach of American power."
The US has long sanctioned Iran, though Tehran has frequently bypassed these restrictions through front companies.
Iran rejects Bessent's 'bombast'
While Bessent was speaking in Washington, the speaker of the Iranian Parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, took to X, saying: "Americans know that no one buys their bombast; the United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries."
"Iran's trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don't take these statements into account anywhere."
US joined Israel in attacking Iran on February 28, with strikes quickly killing the longtime supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and much of the other top brass as well as hundreds of civilians.
But Iran quickly hit back by exerting control over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passageway through which one-fifth of global oil once sailed, and it has rained missiles and drones on US-allied Gulf Arab monarchies, shattering the oil-rich countries' hard-earned reputation for stability.
Tehran has reported thousands of Iranian fatalities as it struck US bases and assets in the Middle East, while the Pentagon has confirmed 18 deaths in addition to 756 injuries among its personnel during the conflict.

Burnham ups the ante in fight against Russia — and leaves Merz in the shade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:00:17 UTC
02:00:17 KST

Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham poses in front the Wall of Remembrance at Mykhailivska Square in Kyiv on Aug. 24, 2026. | Pool photo by Henry Nicholls via WPA/Getty Images
LONDON — Andy Burnham has deepened Britain’s support for Ukraine by boosting the war-torn country’s ability to develop long-range missiles, in his first major move on foreign policy since becoming prime minister.
To mark the PM’s visit to Ukraine — his first overseas trip since taking office last month —Downing Street announced that the U.K. government will allow European defense company MBDA to declassify information about British-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/SCALP missiles in order to help Ukraine build its own version.
The missile initiative puts pressure on German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who had called for German-Swedish Taurus cruise missiles to be given to Ukraine while he was in opposition, only to backtrack after taking office — and who opted out of attending independence day festivities in Kyiv on Monday.
Advertisement
The trip gave Burnham his first chance to show his commitment to the Coalition of the Willing — a grouping of Ukraine’s allies championed by his predecessor, Keir Starmer — as he co-chaired its latest meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron.
Burnham was allowed to enjoy the limelight as the only E3 leader to attend the session in person, with Macron hosting Saudi Arabia’s Mohammed bin Salman and Merz attending to a domestic crisis.
Sitting alongside Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Burnham said Russian threats against the U.K. will not deter him and show British assistance is having an impact.
The British PM said: “It’s clear Russia is running out of options so Putin is now hoping he can win through a campaign of terror using ballistic missiles against Ukrainian civilians.”
The new agreement on missiles is unlikely to have any short-term impact on Russia’s war against Ukraine, but represents a gradual shift in the U.K.’s posture towards deeper cooperation with Kyiv and sharper confrontation with Moscow.
Burnham has also signed a deal allowing the U.K. to access Ukraine’s Avengers AI lab, allowing both sides to collaborate on the development of new battlefield technology, using sensors and cameras to capture and collate information on objects such as tanks, artillery, air defense systems and drone targets.
Advertisement
Speaking in front of St. Sofia Cathedral in Kyiv to mark the 35th anniversary of the nation’s independence, Burnham said: “This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war.”
He vowed that “despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country we will continue our support for Ukraine.”
Turning up the temperature
Germany’s Merz is facing fresh criticism of his stance from within his own parliamentary group, from his coalition partner, and from the opposition. “It’s a clear sign that both countries are no longer waiting for Germany or relying on Germany in this matter,” CDU/CSU foreign policy politician Roderich Kiesewetter told POLITICO.
He added that the British-French initiative was “a call to Germany that, unfortunately, will once again have no effect and also highlights our limited credibility.”
Merz most recently justified his refusal to supply Taurus missiles during a government question session in the Bundestag in March, stating that his support for the idea, expressed while he was in the opposition, had been made “in a different context” — specifically, when Germany had more Taurus missiles for its own defense.
Yet the move comes at a particularly fraught moment for British relations with Russia, after The Times reports that Moscow has withdrawn its ambassador in London without appointing a replacement.
Advertisement
Asked about the decision on British missile technology, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov accused Britain of “methodically and regularly adding fuel to the fire and methodically and regularly plotting to prevent any progress in the peace process.”
Al Carns, a Labour MP who resigned as U.K. armed forces minister earlier this summer over defense funding, told POLITICO the announcement is “a welcome step forward” but should not be seen as an “escalation.” He suggested it is the equivalent of Iran sharing drone technology with Russia.
John Foreman, a former U.K. defense attaché to Russia and Ukraine, said it was “an evolution of position worked out over many months” and “will give Ukraine another string to its bow” at a time when the U.S. is not providing assistance with long-range missiles.
He added: “It shows we won’t be bullied by Russian threats and bluster nor deterred from supporting Ukraine now and in the future.”
A Ukrainian official, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly, hailed Burnham’s show of solidarity as “very significant,” backed up by “a great deliverable.”
The prime minister’s spokesman declined to say the U.K. is adopting a tougher posture, telling journalists: “Our position in support of Ukraine has always been clear. We have invested billions of pounds into helping them win the fight against Russia. We’ve cracked down on Russia in terms of economic sanctions, and that this is a continuation of that stance.”
Advertisement
Words or actions?
The U.K.’s latest announcement has been in train for several months, according to two people with knowledge of the process, and will run alongside Operation Brakestop — the U.K.’s project with Ukraine to develop low-cost long-range strike weapons.
U.K. officials played down any heightened risk of retaliation with Russia, with one senior Whitehall figure, also granted anonymity to speak freely, saying that Moscow’s words did not appear to be matched by any tangible change in their actions.
Matthew Savill, director of military sciences at RUSI, said: “The Russians would almost certainly want to try and locate and destroy any such factory [producing advanced missiles,] but this is hardly an escalation given that SCALP and Storm Shadow were launched at targets inside Russia two years ago, and other Western companies are already assisting with repair and production inside Ukraine.”
This article has been updated. Dan Bloom and Hans von der Burchard contributed reporting.

New partnership set to see the UK and Ukraine develop battle winning technology as Britain secures access to Ukraine's Avengers AI Labs
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
18:00:04 BST
02:00:04 KST

New partnership set to see the UK and Ukraine develop battle winning technology as Britain secures access to Ukraine's Avengers AI Labs
A landmark AI deal between the UK and Ukraine has been signed today as the two countries join forces to develop new military capabilities and the technology of the future.
- UK set to become the first international partner to access Ukraine’s Avengers AI Labs, allowing the two countries to accelerate the development of AI tools to shape the battlefield
- Signed by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Kyiv, the AI Partnership will see the UK back Ukraine with world-leading universities, researchers, technology companies and third largest AI eco-system in the world
- Forms key part of the UK and Ukraine’s 100 Year Partnership and comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham announces that defence firm MBDA can release classified information on UK components for the long-range missile, SCALP
A landmark AI deal between the UK and Ukraine has been signed today as the two countries join forces to develop new military capabilities and the technology of the future.
Bringing together Britain’s world-leading AI ecosystem with Ukraine’s operational experience, engineering talent and technological innovation, the new deal signed by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Ukraine today will enable access to Ukraine’s coveted Avengers AI Labs database.
The platform provides real world data and insights to train AI models, collected by thousands of daylight cameras and infrared sensors across the battlefield in Ukraine.
Those sensors and cameras capture millions of objects, such as tanks, artillery, air defence systems, infantry, and aerial targets, including Shahed drones and reconnaissance UAVs, feeding back data to the Avengers Lab to train new AI models.
With potential to revolutionise all parts of public life, from air traffic control to train systems, the deal will first focus on defence and national security – bringing together engineers, academics, businesses and military operational expertise from both countries to act as an AI cell to solve key national security challenges for both countries.
The partnership will also see the UK and Ukraine explore further platforms to collaborate on.
A goldmine of battlefield data, Avengers AI Labs will give British innovators and researchers unparalleled access to real-world operational insights and the opportunity to ‘plug and play’.
In return, the UK will back Ukraine with world-leading universities, researchers, technology companies and third largest AI eco-system in the world, allowing Ukraine to draw on British expertise to accelerate the development of solutions to urgent challenges, whilst transforming hard-earned operational experience and unique datasets into technologies with long-term benefits for both countries.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:
  Ukraine has become one of the world’s leading innovators in defence technology, forged through courage, ingenuity and the hard lessons of war.
This groundbreaking partnership will bring together Ukraine’s unrivalled operational experience with Britain’s world-class AI ecosystem, giving us the opportunity to develop the technologies of the future, changing lives here in Britain and saving lives on the battlefield in Ukraine.
By combining Ukrainian battlefield data with British expertise, we will accelerate the development of capabilities that not only strengthen our national security but better protect our critical infrastructure and growth in every postcode here at home.
As part of the agreement, several pilot projects have been rolled out with three British startups including Bristol’s Sintela, Oxford’s Mind Foundry and London’s Skyral.
The first of the trial technology is about to be rolled out at a UK defence site to protect bases from protestors and hostile actors trying to gain intelligence.
The project, which uses Ukrainian data and UK technology, turns buried fibre-optic cables into a giant AI-enabled sensor. As well as military bases, the technology could be rolled out to protect airports, prisons and even railways and energy plants in the future.
The second project will see the UK and Ukraine explore the development of next-generation low-power AI chips designed to power future drones, robotics and autonomous systems.
If successful, the technology could underpin a new generation of intelligent machines capable of operating for longer, responding faster and functioning in environments where conventional systems struggle.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said:
  Ukraine is pushing the frontier of defence innovation as they bravely resist Putin’s illegal invasion. From supporting with military equipment and training to co-developing cutting-edge technology, the UK will stand shoulder-to-shoulder with Ukraine for as long as it takes.
By combining the UK’s world-leading scientists, engineers and tech companies with Ukraine’s unique battlefield experience and data, we will strengthen both of our nations’ defence and security.
The deal, which forms a key part of the UK and Ukraine’s 100 Year Partnership, underlines the close relationship between both countries to drive global security and stability and ensure Ukraine has the capability and means to defend itself from Russia’s barbaric invasion.
It also comes after the Prime Minister announced that the UK has agreed that defence firm MBDA can release classified information on UK components for the long-range missile, SCALP, to establish local assembly lines in Ukraine.
Minister for AI, Kanishka Narayan said:
  Britain and Ukraine are the closest of partners. Ukraine’s extraordinary courage on the battlefield has been matched by remarkable technological ingenuity.
“By giving British start-ups, researchers and engineers access to insights from its Avengers AI platform, we are taking that partnership further and helping Britain develop the next generation of defence technology.
This is AI sovereignty in practice: building our own capabilities and turning frontline experience into systems that protect our armed forces overseas and our critical infrastructure at home.

MOSCOW, August 24. /TASS/. Household funds held in Russian banks edged up by 0.3%, or 0.2 trillion rubles ($2.39 bln), in July compared with June amid high demand for cash, according to materials from the Bank of Russia.
"Household funds increased by 0.2 trillion rubles in July (+0.3%, the same as in June). This moderate growth may be associated with increased consumer activity and persistently high demand for cash (the amount of cash in circulation rose by 0.7 trillion rubles in July after increasing by 0.5 trillion rubles in June)," the regulator noted.
On an annual basis, household funds held in banks increased by 9.5% in July, reaching 68.4 trillion rubles ($815.74 bln).
Funds held by legal entities in banks increased by 0.4 trillion rubles ($4.77 bln), or 0.6%, in July after declining by 0.01% in June, despite substantial dividend payments. According to the Bank of Russia, the increase was driven primarily by exporting companies.
Funds held in escrow accounts declined by 60 bln rubles ($716 mln) in July, or 0.8%, after rising by 1.2% in June: the volume of escrow account releases increased, while mortgage lending cooled somewhat.

Sick of getting unsolicited beauty tips on social media, the Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, rebuffed a male cosmetic surgeon’s offer to “fix” her and advised women in similar situations to embrace self-acceptance.
Frederiksen, a Social Democrat and Denmark’s second female prime minister, posted on Instagram that she had just returned from a trip to Ukraine, where she was subjected to air raid sirens, when she found a message proposing some help with her appearance.
She included a screenshot of the exchange in which the doctor, who was not identified, said he could “fix that little spot on your nose”.
Her retort was swift and pointed: “Oh no. I’m happy with my body – I really don’t need a male plastic surgeon to have an opinion about it!”
Frederiksen, who has led the EU and Nato member country since 2019 and is one Europe’s longest-serving heads of government, said being a woman in the public eye meant regular exposure to such unwanted and superficial scrutiny.
“I’ve lost count of how many messages I’ve received over the years about my appearance,” the 48-year-old wrote. “Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly ‘wart’ on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox.”
Frederiksen’s global profile has grown this year as she stood up to US president’s repeated claims on Greenland, a semi-autonomous Danish territory. She is also a staunch supporter of Ukraine against the Russian onslaught.
In a moment of striking candour, Frederiksen admitted annoyance with pushy beauty advice while offering her own guidance how to deal with it.
She said she did not volunteer opinions about other people’s looks and said that “I’m perfectly fine with my body – as it is when you’re a woman approaching 50.”
Frederiksen said she was fine to stay in conversation with the public on a range of topics but encouraged Danes to set the bar higher with their chosen subject matter.
“If you’re going to write to me (and you’re more than welcome to), I hope you’ll use your time to talk about something more meaningful,” she said. “Not my nose.”
Although the mean-spirited suggestions made her feel “indignant”, she said, “today, I’m sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the ‘perfect imperfections’ we all walk around with every day.”

Under the decree, ownership powers would transfer to Russia’s Federal Agency for State Property Management or another designated body, which would take responsibility for the site’s safety and could conduct an inventory of its assets.
Fuel and energy facilities, including nuclear power, are included under the legislation as well as industry, communications, transport and logistics, public utilities and other facilities deemed essential to state security and economic stability.

Ukraine’s Drones Reach Russia’s ICBM and Military Satellite Launch Hub for First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:56:19 UTC
01:56:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Drones Reach Russia’s ICBM and Military Satellite Launch Hub for First Time
Ukrainian drones reached Russia’s northern Arkhangelsk region, home to the strategic Plesetsk military cosmodrome used to launch military satellites and intercontinental ballistic missiles, according to OSINT analysis published by Russian independent media outlet Astra on August 23.
The incident appears to mark the first documented case of Ukrainian drones reaching the Arkhangelsk region, extending Kyiv’s deep-strike reach into Russia’s far north.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian monitoring resource Locator Rossii reported that at least two drones reached the Plesetsk area.
ASTRA analyzed photographs taken by local residents and said smoke could be seen rising in the vicinity of the military spaceport. The images were reportedly taken from Mirny, a closed city established during the Soviet era specifically to support operations at Plesetsk.
The exact target and consequences of the reported drone operation remain unclear.
Astra also geolocated footage published by Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ showing a drone flying above Kargopol in the Arkhangelsk region. The aircraft was traveling in the direction of Plesetsk, located roughly 170 kilometers, or 105 miles, away.
Local residents separately recorded two drones flying through the region and posted footage of the aircraft online.
Temporary flight restrictions were introduced at an airfield near the Plesetsk Cosmodrome because of the potential drone threat, under Russia’s emergency airspace closure procedure known as the Carpet Plan.
Plesetsk is Russia’s principal northern military spaceport and plays a significant role in both its military space program and strategic missile testing.
Russia has repeatedly launched Soyuz-2 and Angara rockets carrying military spacecraft from the facility. The cosmodrome is also being used to deploy Rassvet communications satellites, part of Moscow’s effort to build a domestic satellite internet network comparable to SpaceX’s Starlink.
Russia plans to have 292 Rassvet communications satellites in orbit by the end of 2027, making the program increasingly important for Moscow’s communications infrastructure.
Plesetsk also serves a separate strategic military role as a launch site for Russian intercontinental ballistic missiles.
No confirmed information has yet emerged regarding damage at the cosmodrome or whether Plesetsk was the drones’ intended target.
Russia continues to deploy its “Rassvet” satellite constellation, which is intended to serve as an analogue to Starlink.
However, the project requires regular launches of carrier rockets. The first two groups of Rassvet satellites were launched into orbit using Soyuz-2.1b rockets manufactured by the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara.
Production of carrier rockets is one of the key constraints on the deployment of the constellation. The satellites can also be launched from the Plesetsk and Vostochny spaceports in Russia, as well as the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

Tehran warns countries supporting US military actions of consequences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:54:59 UTC
01:54:59 KST

Tehran warns countries supporting US military actions of consequences
TEHRAN — Iran warned on Monday that countries allowing the United States or Israel to use their military bases, facilities or equipment for operations against Iran could face consequences, as Tehran hardened its position over the ongoing regional crisis and rejected any attempt to end the conflict on terms dictated by its adversaries.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said Iran’s diplomatic strategy was being adjusted to reflect changing regional and international conditions, while emphasizing that Tehran would continue using bilateral and multilateral channels to defend what it considers its national interests, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Speaking at his weekly press conference in Tehran, Baqaei said Iran could not rely on diplomatic methods developed under different circumstances and needed to continuously strengthen its diplomatic capabilities. He described the US campaign of economic pressure as “economic warfare” and said Tehran had repeatedly characterized such measures as economic terrorism.
The spokesperson said Washington was using multiple forms of pressure against Iranians because of their insistence on national sovereignty, independence and dignity. He warned that Iran had already issued, and would continue to issue, warnings concerning countries that cooperate with US actions against the Islamic Republic.
Tehran rejects war settlement dictated by aggressor
The Iranian spokesman also sought to clarify President Masoud Pezeshkian’s recent comments that it would be preferable to end the war while Iran was in a position of strength.
Baqaei rejected interpretations that the remarks indicated Tehran was prepared to make concessions to its adversaries. He said Iran had not initiated the conflict and would not permit the war to end on conditions imposed by the party responsible for the aggression.
“We will show no leniency toward the aggressors,” Baqaei said, arguing that Iran had been defending its territorial integrity and national sovereignty. He added that the aggressor should be held accountable.
According to Baqaei, the Iranian leadership had repeatedly made clear that the country would not surrender to coercion or domination. He said the government and all branches of the Iranian state had acted with unity during the 40-day conflict as well as during an earlier 12-day war.
The remarks underscore Tehran’s insistence that any future diplomatic process must take place without what it regards as coercive demands from Washington or its allies.
The spokesman also criticized the United States for what he described as repeated breaches of commitments in previous negotiations, including the 2015 nuclear agreement and other diplomatic understandings. He said Iran had repeatedly responded to what it considered goodwill gestures from Tehran with broken promises.
Warning to countries providing bases
Baqaei issued one of his strongest warnings to countries whose military infrastructure could be used by the United States or Israel in operations against Iran.
Responding to reports concerning American military facilities and aircraft in European countries, he said Tehran had previously made clear its position on Bulgaria and confirmed reports that several US KC-135 refueling aircraft had departed the country.
Baqaei argued that allowing foreign military forces to use national bases and facilities for attacks on Iran could amount to participation in aggression under international law. He said Iran had no dispute with the people of Bulgaria but viewed the use of facilities there in support of US and Israeli military operations as problematic.
He further warned that Iran considered itself entitled to respond against the source of an attack.
“It is Iran’s right to target the source and origin of any act of aggression,” Baqaei said, adding that Tehran would show no leniency in defending the country.
The warning comes amid heightened sensitivity over the role of foreign military bases and logistical facilities in any potential resumption of hostilities.
Strait of Hormuz becomes a key flashpoint
The Strait of Hormuz was another major focus of the briefing, with Baqaei rejecting claims in US media and official circles that the strategic waterway had become fully open to shipping.
He disputed reports citing oil flows ranging from 5 million to 17 million barrels per day and claims of a sharp increase in maritime traffic. Baqaei described the figures as part of what he called a media and psychological campaign, arguing that insecurity created by US and Israeli actions had affected conditions in the region and around the strait since February 28, 2026.
The comments highlight the strategic importance of Hormuz, through which a significant share of global energy supplies normally passes, and signal that Tehran continues to regard security and traffic through the waterway as closely linked to the wider regional conflict.
Baqaei said Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi, who was scheduled to visit Tehran, would discuss bilateral relations as well as security and shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, he rejected suggestions that the Omani visit was connected to the simultaneous visit by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir.
Diplomacy continues amid economic pressure
Despite the confrontational rhetoric, Tehran said diplomatic engagement with neighboring countries remained active.
Baqaei described relations with Pakistan as being at their strongest stages and said Munir’s visit was aimed at further expanding bilateral ties. He also pointed to efforts to improve economic relations with Afghanistan, including reducing border and customs barriers.
He said a meeting between Afghan Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs Mullah Baradar and President Pezeshkian had addressed ways of facilitating economic cooperation, adding that measures to remove obstacles to trade had subsequently been placed on the agenda.
Iran is also dealing with the consequences of US economic pressure and damage to its energy infrastructure. Baqaei said the government was taking the necessary measures to meet winter energy requirements, with the Oil Ministry handling technical preparations and the Foreign Ministry engaging with countries capable of supplying energy if needed.
He accused Washington of seeking to undermine Iran’s sovereignty while also damaging the international free-trade system by pressuring other countries to restrict commerce with Tehran. He called such pressure a violation of international relations and the principles of the U.N. Charter.
Tehran maintains regional policy
Baqaei also reaffirmed Iran’s opposition to Israel’s occupation and military presence in the region, describing resistance to what Tehran calls Zionist occupation as a principled element of Iranian foreign policy.
He said Iran’s position was not dependent on which political group or faction governed other Islamic countries and reiterated Tehran’s opposition to what it described as continued Israeli occupation and aggression in Syria.
At the same time, Baqaei denied reports that Iran had received an official invitation to join a proposed trilateral defense arrangement involving Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. He said regional proposals presented to Tehran so far had centered on dialogue, consultations and collective security rather than formal membership in a new defense bloc.

France readies high school phone ban for September
Unknown

France readies high school phone ban for September
- France will enforce a ban on mobile phone use in high schools starting September, as part of President Macron's effort to reduce screen time among children.
- Many schools face challenges implementing the ban quickly due to short preparation time and the need to update internal regulations.
- Exemptions are allowed for educational purposes, and the government plans new laws to restrict social media access for children under 15 by next spring.
AI generated
PARIS - The French government said on Aug 24 it would press ahead with a ban on mobile phones in high schools from September, but trade unions warned that the measure might be hard to implement quickly.
In July, France’s Parliament approved legislation banning both social media access for children under 15 and mobile phone use in high schools.
It is part of a push by President Emmanuel Macron for children to spend less time in front of screens, which the government fears is arresting their development.
But earlier this month, the country’s top court struck down the social media provision, dealing a blow to Macron.
However, the Constitutional Council did not rule on the separate provision banning mobile phone use in high schools.
On Aug 24, government spokesperson Maud Bregeon said Macron “has decided to promulgate the law” containing the ban on phones, despite the Constitutional Council striking down its flagship provision.
“As a result, the ban on mobile phones in high schools can take effect from the start of the new school year, with a stable, consolidated and statutory legal framework,” she said, after a Cabinet meeting.
France’s school year starts in September.
France has already banned children from using mobile phones in colleges – the schools attended between the ages of 11 and 15 – and in primary schools.
In early July, high schools had been instructed to prepare for the measure’s implementation in September, ahead of its adoption by parliament later that month.
In order to enforce the ban, schools must amend their internal regulations.
‘Not ready’
But many schools may struggle to implement the measure because they have had little time to prepare.
Francois Resnais, national secretary of SNPDEN-Unsa, France’s top union of school principals, criticised the timing as “bad”.
“Schools are not ready,” Resnais told AFP.
“Schools are starting the year with a rule that is not written into their internal regulations, except perhaps for those that tried to anticipate something, but that remains very limited.”
Christelle Kauffmann, the union’s deputy secretary-general, is among the minority of school leaders who anticipated the measure.
At her high school, phones will be banned in corridors and school buildings from the start of term, but allowed outdoors.
She said it could take nearly a year before the ban could be fully implemented across all high schools.
“It is very difficult for a school community to impose a new rule on young people. Even if the law is supposed to apply automatically, it is not that simple,” she said. “You cannot put a supervisor behind every student.”
Kamel Chibli, vice-president of the Occitanie regional council in southern France, said digital pouches and lockers used to store smartphones cost the regional authorities around 40,000 euros for a high school with 1,500 students.
High school students regularly use their smartphones to check timetable changes, room assignments and other school information. Some teachers also rely on phones in class for research, exercises and document sharing.
In its guidance, the education ministry allows exemptions from the ban for “educational uses” or for purposes “necessary for the proper functioning of the school”.
Macron’s office has said the president has no plans to give up on his push to bar children from apps such as TikTok and the government would work on a new draft law.
“The president’s objective is to have a stable legal framework in place by next spring to protect our children and young people,” said Bregeon.
Macron is due to step down in spring 2027 after serving the maximum two consecutive terms allowed in office. AFP

The Ministerial Committee for Shin Bet Affairs approved on July 16 lifetime security protection for Netanyahu, while his wife, Sara, will be protected for as long as her husband is alive. The prime minister’s sons will continue to receive security protection for five years even after he leaves office. Since their protection has currently been approved through the end of 2026, the service will effectively continue until late 2031.
According to various sources, security officials, including the Shin Bet and Mossad, have determined that Netanyahu and his family will remain under a high-level threat for the rest of their lives because of the desire by Israel’s enemies to avenge operations and targeted killings carried out during the war.

Astros and GM Dana Brown mutually agree to part ways
HOUSTON (AP) — General manager Dana Brown and the Houston Astros have mutually agreed to part ways, the team announced Monday, when it was tied for first place in the AL West.
Brown’s contract was set to expire at the end of the season. Senior adviser Jeff Bagwell and assistant general managers Charles Cook, Gavin Dickey and Connor Huff will take over Brown’s responsibilities while team owner Jim Crane will oversee baseball operations during the transition.
The move comes after the Astros went 3-6 on a homestand that ended Sunday to fall into a tie with the Texas Rangers for the AL West lead.
Brown had been the team’s general manager since January 2023.
“Over the past four seasons, Dana has helped our organization win two division titles and has led our baseball front office through key scouting, draft and development efforts,” Crane said in a statement. “On behalf of the Astros, I want to thank him for his commitment, energy, and contributions to our organization. We wish he and his family the best.”
Brown came to Houston after four seasons as vice president of scouting for the Atlanta Braves to replace James Click, who was not given a new contract and left the Astros just days after they won the 2022 World Series.
“I want to thank Jim Crane for the opportunity to serve in my first role as an MLB General Manager,” Brown said. “The Astros organization and the fans have welcomed me and my family, and I am grateful to have called Houston home for the past four seasons. I wish the organization well and I look forward to the future as I continue my 36-plus years in professional baseball.”

Open letter on Iranian prisoners draws criticism over its framing of war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:51:48 UTC
01:51:48 KST

Open letter on Iranian prisoners draws criticism over its framing of war
TEHRAN- An open letter signed by a group of Western academics, writers, activists and former and current political prisoners has drawn criticism from other scholars and anti-war activists, who argue that its focus on Iran’s domestic developments risks obscuring the central issue of the conflict: the foreign military assault on the country.
The letter, addressed to what it calls Iran’s “prisoners of conscience,” condemns executions, arbitrary arrests, torture, alleged sham trials and the targeting of ethnic minorities. It describes Iranian political prisoners as being caught “between two blades of a scissors” — one representing the Islamic Republic and the other the United States and Israel.
The signatories call on the Iranian authorities to end executions and release political prisoners, while also calling on Washington and Israel to end what they describe as their “barbaric wars and brutal sanctions.”
The list of signatories includes figures such as Angela Davis, Mumia Abu-Jamal, Judith Butler, Rashid Khalidi, Robin D. G. Kelley, Ruth Wilson Gilmore and Walden Bello, among others.
 
 Yet the letter has prompted a broader debate over whether placing Iran’s political prisoners at the center of the discussion, while the country is under military attack, creates a misleading equivalence between domestic developments and an external war.
Critics question the letter’s political framing
One critic, writing under the name Carlos on X, described the letter as politically problematic despite believing that its signatories included people with long records of opposition to imperialism and political repression.
Noting the participation of figures including Davis, Abu-Jamal, Khalidi, Kelley, Gilmore and Butler, Carlos wrote that these were not people who could simply be dismissed; several had spent their lives in anti-imperialist and Black liberation movements.
But he argued that the letter nevertheless adopted 'a misleading framework.'
Its central metaphor, he wrote, was the image of the Islamic Republic on one side and US-Israeli imperialism on the other, with the Iranian people caught between them. According to Carlos, the framing “inserts a symmetry” between the two sides while failing to adequately distinguish between a state facing an external military attack and the domestic political system governing it.
Carlos also questioned the timing and potential political consequences of the letter. He argued that, regardless of what individual signatories intended, the text could function as part of a broader political narrative used to justify pressure on Iran.
He specifically criticized the letter for invoking allegations including sham trials, systematic torture and the targeting of minorities without providing detailed sourcing in the text. He argued that similar language has historically been used in campaigns preceding regime-change efforts.
His criticism was echoed, in a different form, by Ajamu Baraka, an international human-rights activist and political organizer. Baraka did not reject criticism of Iran itself. Instead, he distinguished between criticizing a government and taking a political position in the context of war.
“No one is above criticism,” Baraka wrote. “Comrades who signed that letter need to understand the difference between criticism & political positioning.”
He argued that the signatories had chosen a political position that, in his view, gave legitimacy to U.S. military violence against Iran.
The reaction from legal scholar Nina Farnia was also critical. Farnia shared material relating to the letter while defending her own position on the conflict. Her broader intervention questioned the decision by progressive voices in the United States and elsewhere to focus publicly on condemning Iran at a moment when, in her view, greater attention should be directed toward opposing the war and sanctions imposed by their own governments.
Historian and scholar Adnan A. Husain similarly questioned the political timing of the letter. In a post responding to the debate, he maintained that publishing an open letter focused on condemning Iran, while the United States and Israel were engaged in military and economic pressure against the country, risked shifting political attention away from opposition to the war.
Husain wrote that the Western left was moving toward public condemnation of Iran “just when” the United States was turning increasingly to economic pressure and political subversion. He argued that activists should instead organize against the war and sanctions imposed by their own government.
David Miller, Political sociologist, producer, and former professor at the University of Bristol said, all signed the disgraceful letter to the Guardian denouncing the Islamic Republic of Iran, the world’s leading anti-imperialist state.
Worse, they compare the Republic with the Zionist/US imperialist aggressor. What we (and they) should be doing is defending the Republic. The Islamic Republic of Iran is not only defending itself, the Palestinians, Lebanon, and the resistance movement. It’s also defending all of humanity and indeed civilization against the depredations of Jewish supremacist imperialism. This is an existential matter for the whole world.
Susan Abulhawa, Palestinian author and activist, has issued a sharp critique of mainstream framing that portrays the US-Israeli confrontation with Iran as a balanced conflict between two equal sides.
In a statement shared on her platform, Abulhawa argues that such framing ignores a "profound asymmetry of power." She describes Iran as a nation crippled by decades of sanctions, now fighting an "existential anti-imperial struggle," while facing a nuclear-armed U.S.-Israeli empire with unlimited military resources, surveillance, and near-total dominance over global political, legal, and information systems.
Abulhawa takes issue with minimizing language in a recent letter, which referred to "current, indiscriminate waves of US-Israeli military assaults." She says that this understates the scale of destruction, citing unprovoked attacks on a school that killed 180 children and teachers, the assassination of Iran's spiritual leader and much of its leadership, and strikes on civilian infrastructure including water systems, farmland, and power grids. She also highlights the downing of Iran Air Flight 655 by the U.S., which killed 290 civilians, and decades of assassinations of Iranian scientists and commanders—all of which went unanswered.
The activist also criticizes the letter for failing to contextualize Iranian arrests of detainees, arguing that while some imprisonments may be wrongful, others involve individuals who confessed to espionage for Mossad or terrorism, including a group that brutally murdered a young Quran reciter. She insists that any fair assessment must engage with Iran's legitimate security concerns.
Abulhawa concludes that the conflict is not a symmetrical confrontation but an anti-imperial struggle against overwhelming imperial force distinction, she says, is crucial for honest analysis.
Questions over the signatories’ motives and the letter’s focus
Without direct statements from each signatory, it would be difficult to establish that they all interpreted the letter in precisely the same way.
The criticism therefore raises a legitimate journalistic question rather than providing a definitive answer: what exactly did each signatory intend to endorse?
That question is particularly relevant because the letter was published during a period of military confrontation. The document gives substantial attention to Iran’s domestic political developments, while the external conflict appears largely as one half of a broader framework of “dual oppression.”
For critics, this framing risks placing the government of a country under attack and the states conducting military operations against it within a single conceptual structure, without sufficiently addressing the different forms of power and responsibility involved.
But the timing and framing matter. A government’s policy inside the country and another state’s decision to wage war against that country are separate questions. They can both be condemned, but they carry different legal, political, and moral implications. Treating them as interchangeable risks obscuring the question of responsibility for the conflict itself.
The debate over the letter therefore goes beyond Iran’s domestic politics. It raises a broader question for international intellectual and human-rights circles: how should activists respond when a country facing external military attack is also accused of serious internal repression?
What remains less clear is whether all those whose names appear beneath the letter share the same interpretation of that argument.
That uncertainty is itself significant. The prominence of the signatories may lend the letter considerable political weight, but a list of names cannot, by itself, establish a uniform political position. Determining what each individual intended to endorse would require direct confirmation from the signatories themselves.
Its critics, however, contend that the document’s framing places the aggressor and the state under attack within an overly symmetrical narrative and risks diverting attention from the central question of the war: who initiated the military action, what legal basis was claimed for it, and who bears responsibility for its consequences?

Russians overstate the number of aircraft launched over their territory by an average of 3–4 times – Fire Point CEO
Kyiv • UNN
Russia overstates by an average of 3–4 times the number of strike aircraft allegedly shot down over its territory. Fire Point urged people not to rely on these figures.
Russians overestimate by an average of 3–4 times the number of strike aircraft launched at their territory. It all depends on what kind of "drama" they need to demonstrate. This was stated by Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh, UNN reports.
"We once analyzed single-target missions, where we knew that only our aircraft were flying. On average, the Russians inflated the number of aircraft launched there by 3–4 times and then reported them as shot down," Iryna Terekh said on the YouTube channel "SBS: Unmanned Systems Forces."
According to her, the figures provided by the Russians vary depending on "what kind of drama needs to be stirred up."
"For example, there was a successful mission that required two Flamingos, yes, and both reached the target, while they wrote: "18, 20, 35 Flamingos shot down." The same applies to drones. Therefore, the scariest thing is when our journalists rely on Russian figures to somehow make calculations," Iryna Terekh noted.
Let us recall
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy called for an increase in the number of FP-5 Flamingo missiles produced by the Ukrainian company Fire Point, which are used to strike facilities in the Russian rear.
"Thousands of our Deep Strikes have already been seen by moscow, tuapse, tula, ryazan, olenya, omsk, and dozens of other points that our Ukrainian justice has already reached. Russia must see more of this justice. "Flamingos" should not be a rare species but a common bird; they should winter in Russia," the head of state noted.
The FP-5 "Flamingo" is a modern ground-based UAV/cruise missile system, designed to deliver a specified payload of up to 1,150 kg to strike ground targets with fixed topographic coordinates at a range of up to 3,000 km, both day and night. The missile can hit a target even amid active electronic warfare.
Fire Point emphasizes that the FP-5 stands out for its ease of use and low cost. It is the largest system in its class, but remains simple to manufacture and launch. It does not require expensive launch platforms—its launchers are reusable, making deployment more economical.
The company also produces the long-range FP-1 and FP-2 drones.

How Syria's skies are becoming a new Israel-Turkey battleground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:46:45 UTC
01:46:45 KST

Breadcrumb
How Syria's skies are becoming a new Israel-Turkey battleground
On 18 August, Israeli fighter jets struck a northwestern Syrian airfield eight times, with Tel Aviv claiming it had pre-empted a Turkish military deployment there.
While the raid did not result in a clash between the two powerful militaries, it nevertheless demonstrated once again how Syria essentially has no control over its airspace.
The airstrikes hit Syria’s Abu al-Duhur Air Base, causing damage but no casualties. Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shaibani said that Turkish military officers visited the site days before the strike. Turkey denied that any delegation was at the base before or during the attack.
Israel claimed Turkey was “on the verge of breaching” the “status quo in security matters” by deploying troops, with Ankara, in turn, describing Israel’s actions as an “unacceptable” and “reckless” threat to regional peace and stability.
Israel previously bombed three airbases in central Syria in April 2025 shortly after Turkey scoped them for potentially deploying forces.
All of these incidents highlight how Syria’s airspace, far from being under its sovereign control, is being contested by its two powerful neighbours who both have large American-equipped air forces.
While Israel appears predominant for now, Turkey may seek to incrementally put constraints on its rival’s aerial supremacy over its southern neighbour.
The battle over Syria's airspace
“The pressure on Israel’s freedom of action in Syria appears to be increasing, even if it has not yet produced a decisive constraint,” Muaz Al Abdullah, Middle East Research Manager at the non-profit Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, told The New Arab.
He noted that the Trump administration has signalled an effort to broaden the Abraham Accords to include Syria “while reducing the scope of conflicts” involving Israel, and the US by extension, in the Middle East. “That diplomatic backdrop coincides with a visible change on the ground,” Abdullah said.
ACLED data shows a notable decline in Israeli airstrikes in Syria since August 2025. Abdullah assesses that this might mean the “operational window” Israel enjoyed since the former regime of Bashar Al-Assad collapsed in December 2024 is beginning to narrow.
“The broader picture, however, is more mixed: Israeli incursions and violence against civilians have continued in uneven but persistent patterns,” Abdullah told The New Arab.
“The shift suggests that Israel may be relying more heavily on ground incursions and other forms of pressure to meet its immediate security objectives,” he added.
“Airstrikes, by contrast, appear to be reserved for moments when those measures are deemed insufficient, as reflected in strikes against Abu al-Duhur, T4, Tadmor, and Hama airbases.”
Replacing Russia's role?
Before the dramatic, free-fall collapse of the brutal Assad regime, Russia officially controlled much of Syria’s airspace around regime-controlled areas and bombed opposition-held regions like Idlib.
Shortly after Russia intervened in Syria’s civil war in September 2015, it established a deconfliction mechanism with Israel, allowing the Israeli Air Force to continue striking suspected Iranian assets in the war-torn country.
US Special Envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said after Israel’s latest strike that the US is working on a similar mechanism between Israel, Turkey, and Syria to reduce the risk of clashes.
Suleyman Ozeren, a lecturer at the American University and senior fellow at the Orion Policy Institute, doesn’t believe this necessarily indicates that Turkey is replacing Russia’s pre-2024 role in Syria or will ever replace it.
“Unlike Russia, Turkey, at least for now, does not appear capable of deterring Israel from carrying out military incursions and strikes inside Syria,” Ozeren told The New Arab.
“Israel’s decision to bomb Abu al-Duhur Air Base, located relatively close to the Turkish-Syrian border, sends a clear message to both the (Syrian President Ahmed) al-Sharaa government and Ankara,” he added.
“Although Turkey responded to the incident with a relatively restrained protest, the strike itself is a troubling indication of how quickly tensions between Israel and Turkey could escalate.”
Deconfliction and de-escalation
Kristin Ronzi, a Middle East and North Africa analyst at the risk intelligence company RANE, says the Turkish-Israeli deconfliction mechanism has already helped de-escalate tensions between the two countries in Syria and “mitigate the risk” of miscalculation.
“As such, Turkey has maintained significant influence over Syrian airspace in the north, while Israel has influence in the south,” Ronzi told The New Arab.
“Even so, the early 18 August Israeli airstrikes against Abu al-Duhur military base in northwestern Syria indicate that Israel is able to extend its operations further into Syria.”
She noted that Barrack’s description of the Israeli strikes as “unnecessary escalation” indicates a limited US tolerance for Israeli airstrikes in Syria in light of warming US-Syria ties and concerns over “Turkish-Israeli frictions”.
“The Trump administration will likely tolerate Israel’s military presence in southern Syria and sporadic ground incursions,” Ronzi said. “But the United States will likely pressure Israel to restrict airstrikes, especially against targets that do not pose a national security threat and risk elevating Syrian-Israeli tensions,” the analyst added.
“Syria will rhetorically reject Israeli violations of its airspace; Syria will be unwilling and unable to effectively control its airspace.”
ACLED’s Abdullah expects that the present status quo of Israel dominating Syria’s southern and central airspace without “direct contestation” with Turkey in central Syria, where there are overlapping areas of influence, will hold.
He recalled Israel’s airstrikes against central Syrian airbases in April 2025 to deter Turkey from establishing any presence.
“The recent strike on Abu al-Duhur does not necessarily represent a contest for dominance between Israel and Turkey in northern Syria,” he said. “It is better understood as a matter of undeclared areas of influence between the two sides, alongside Israeli political objectives tied to the domestic situation inside Israel,” Abdullah added.
“At the same time, where Turkish and Israeli influence in Syria begins and ends is a separate question from Israel’s deterrence strategy of preventing Syria from acquiring an effective, modern air force. That strategy is also one of the reasons behind the Abu al-Duhur strike.”
Ronzi believes Israel will likely reject any Turkish efforts to expand its military influence any further in central Syria.
“Efforts to enhance Syria’s air defence systems would likely be a red line for Israel and Israel would likely obstruct any such efforts, including potentially through pre-emptive airstrikes as Israel has previously done,” she said.
Dreams of a new Syrian air force
Israel’s post-Assad airstrikes destroyed much of what was left of the old regime’s Russian-built air defences and antiquated air force, including its most advanced fighter jets, the Soviet-era MiG-29.
Syria still has some less advanced flyable jets, including Czech-built L-39 light attack aircraft, two of which performed a flyby in a July graduation ceremony for air force cadets, and vintage Soviet-era Su-22s, two of which were spotted over Idlib this August. Israel opposes Syria reconstituting its air force and air defence.
Israel was even concerned that the installation of an HTRS-100 Air Traffic Control Radar System built by Turkey’s Aselsan at Damascus International Airport in January could challenge its air supremacy over Syria.
Ronzi noted that while the HTRS-100 has “commercial and civilian benefits,” it nonetheless “raised Israeli concerns” that it could constrain its military operations.
While Turkey might be able to support “limited Syrian air defence infrastructure,” Abdullah predicts that Israel is likely to “draw a clear line” around any capability that could give Damascus any “meaningful independent control” over its skies.
“Israel’s defence doctrine has increasingly rested on keeping neighbouring states unable to threaten it militarily,” he said.
“In that context, Israel may tolerate Turkey’s deployment of the HTRS-100 radar system at Damascus International Airport, but it is expected to resist any further steps that would allow Syrian forces to own or operate effective air capabilities.”
Ozeren noted that maintaining control over Syrian airspace remains a “key security objective” for Israel that increasingly conflicts with Turkey’s ambitions to expand its influence and presence on the ground in that country.
“Syrian airspace, therefore, is likely to become a major arena in which the competing objectives of Israel and Turkey are tested,” he said. “Without meaningful US intervention, tensions between Israel and Turkey could escalate further.”
“If this competition becomes prolonged, Damascus may eventually seek a more formidable external partner capable of balancing these pressures,” he added. “In that context, a renewed reliance on Russia, though seemingly implausible today, could become a more viable option in the near future.”
ACLED’s Abdullah anticipates that Damascus is likely to turn to Ankara for help in any attempt to rebuild the country’s air force. The expanding partnership between the two makes such cooperation plausible. Turkey could provide pilot training, aircraft, and technical support.
“Recent developments suggest that Syria is already preparing for that possibility,” he said. “The graduation of more than 1,000 non-commissioned officers from the Syrian Air Force Academy points to a broader effort to restore the country’s air arm.”
However, what type of aircraft Syria might seek from Turkey remains uncertain. Furthermore, any procurement decision Damascus ultimately makes will likely be shaped by financial constraints and red lines imposed by Israel.
“Syria may also choose to invest more heavily in unmanned systems rather than trying to rebuild a conventional fighter fleet from the ground up,” Abdullah told The New Arab. “Turkey has a clear advantage in drones, and Syrian forces already have experience that Ankara could help develop,” he added.
“Such a strategy would allow Damascus to challenge Israeli dominance indirectly, without attempting to match Israel in the manned-fighter arena.”
RANE’s Ronzi recalled that Israel’s ferocious attacks on weapons caches and the remnants of Assad’s military following the regime collapse significantly degraded any new military threat his successor can pose to Israel.
“Rebuilding the Syrian Air Force is not likely to be a near-term priority for the interim Syrian government as it faces numerous domestic threats, including the Islamic State, as well as the task of developing new state institutions, over time,” Ronzi said.
Syria will probably attempt to buy new aircraft to improve its military capabilities, most likely from Turkey.
“Even though Israel would maintain a qualitative military edge over any Syrian air force, Israel will be wary of any Syrian effort to rebuild its air force and concerned about the potential that it could eventually be used against Israel,” Ronzi added.
